entries.narration: This course follows one online shop from an empty account to a running, secured, recoverable system. Before any cloud, here is that shop the old way. A shopper asks for a product page, product one thousand and one. The request crosses the internet to one server in a cupboard, and that one server does everything: it runs the web application, holds the database of products and orders, and stores the product images. On a quiet night this works well. The plot on the right is the shop's day, and it is the same day for the whole course. From midnight to eight in the morning, sixty requests arrive every second. Through the working day, two hundred and forty. In the evening, when people shop from the sofa, five hundred and sixty. The dashed line is what one server can serve: one hundred and fifty requests a second. In the morning the server is mostly idle. By day it is ninety requests a second short, and in the evening it is four hundred and ten short, so pages slow down, then time out, at exactly the hours the shop makes its money. The obvious answer is to buy for the evening: four servers, six hundred requests a second. Now look at the table on the far right. Averaged over the day, the shop asks for two hundred and sixty requests a second, so those four servers are busy forty three percent of the time. More than half of what you bought sits idle, and costs the same whether it is busy or not. Owning the machines brings the other jobs listed on the left. You size them once, for one number, months before you need them. Growing means ordering hardware, waiting for it, and installing it. And when a disk or a power supply fails at two in the morning, the call-out is yours. Nothing here is wrong; it is simply the cost of owning capacity. Next, what changes when you rent it instead.

The cloud's first idea is simple: rent the servers instead of owning them, and rent only as many as the hour needs. On the left is the same shop on rented capacity. A shopper's request now goes to a load balancer, which spreads requests across however many app servers are running. Overnight that is one server. Through the day, two. In the evening, four. Each server is the same as the others, so it does not matter which one answers. The plot shows the result. The demand line is unchanged: sixty, two hundred and forty, then five hundred and sixty requests a second. The solid capacity line now steps up with it, one fifty, then three hundred, then six hundred, always just above demand. The dashed line at the top is the owned alternative, four servers all day. The table puts a price on the gap. Owning for the peak means four servers for twenty four hours: ninety six server-hours. Following demand means one server for eight hours, two for ten and four for six: fifty two server-hours. At a hypothetical four cents per server-hour, a rate this course uses throughout and always labels as invented, that is three dollars eighty four a day against two dollars and eight cents. That ability to grow and shrink with demand is called elasticity, and renting by the hour or second is called on-demand. The list on the left says what it needs. A new server must be a request to an A P I, ready in minutes rather than months. You must pay only while a server runs. Every server must be able to take any request, which is a property of the application, and Course six makes the shop's app behave that way. And because adding a server still takes minutes, capacity has to arrive slightly before demand does, which the shop will do with a schedule for the evening peak. Next, the second idea: renting not just machines, but whole services.

Renting servers moves the hardware to A W S, but the shop still runs everything on them. A managed service goes further: A W S runs the software too, and you use it through an A P I. The row across the top is a ladder, from the most work to the least. Each card lists what you still run, and underneath it, what A W S runs for you. On the far left is your own server, where you run all of it: the building, the power, the hardware, the operating system, the database software, and finally your own code and data. One step right is E C two, A W S's virtual machines. The building and hardware are gone from your list, but the operating system, its security patches and any database you install are still yours. Next is R D S, a managed relational database. You no longer install or patch the database engine; you choose its size, its backup settings and the weekly window in which A W S applies patches, and you own the tables, the queries and the data. Then Lambda, which runs a function when something calls it. There are no servers to see at all: you supply the code, its memory, its timeout and its permissions, and A W S keeps the runtime patched. On the right is S Q S, a message queue that is purely a service. You choose its settings and who may use it, and send it messages. Nothing else is yours. The table below says what moving right costs as well as buys. You do fewer jobs, but you give up control: versions, operating system access, deep tuning. You inherit the service's limits, which A W S documents as quotas. And you pay closer to what you use, per request or per gigabyte rather than per machine. The shop uses all four, each where it fits, and the list says where they arrive. Next, how security is split between you and A W S along this same ladder.

Once part of the system belongs to A W S and part to you, every security job needs an owner. A W S calls this the shared responsibility model, and it fits in one sentence: A W S is responsible for security of the cloud, and you are responsible for security in the cloud. On the left are the two halves. A W S secures the cloud itself: the data centres and the people guarding them, the hardware and its disks, the global network, the hypervisor that separates one customer's virtual machines from another's, the Regions and zones, and the software inside every managed service. You secure what you put in it and how you configure it: who may do what, your data and whether it is encrypted, the network rules, your application code, the operating system on any E C two server, and every setting you choose. The table on the right shows that the line moves with the service, which is why the last section mattered. Physical hardware is always A W S. The operating system is yours on E C two, and A W S's on R D S and Lambda. The database engine is yours if you install one on E C two, and A W S patches it on R D S. A Lambda runtime is patched by A W S. But two rows never move. Who may call a resource, and the data inside it, are yours on every service, including S three. The list underneath turns the table into incidents. A disk failing in a data centre is A W S's to fix. A bucket that anyone on the internet can read is yours, because A W S stored exactly what it was told and allowed exactly what you configured. An E C two server that misses a security patch is yours. An R D S engine patch is applied by A W S, in the maintenance window you set. Most cloud security failures sit in your half, and most of this course is about doing that half well. Next, the whole shop we are going to build.

This is the finished shop, on the one map this course keeps returning to. Read it from the top. A shopper's request first reaches the edge: Route fifty three answers the D N S question of where the shop lives, CloudFront serves cached pages from close to the shopper, and a web application firewall filters what gets through. Below is the shop's home: one A W S Region, E U west two in London, inside the production account. In the V P C, the shop's private network, a load balancer spreads requests over the app servers, which read and write the orders database and a cache. To the right is the data: S three buckets for product files and images, a DynamoDB table, a data lake with its catalog, Athena to query it, and a stream of clicks. Underneath is the checkout, built from managed pieces: an A P I in front, a function that places the order, a workflow that coordinates payment and shipping, and a queue, a topic and an event bus that carry the work that happens after the shopper has gone. Around everything, at the bottom, are the parts that touch every other part: the accounts, the I A M roles, the stacks and the pipeline that build and release it, CloudWatch and CloudTrail that record what it does, the K M S keys that encrypt it, the backups, and the cost. The table on the right is the course itself. Each course adds the parts the shop needs next: a first bucket and a cost ledger in Course three, accounts and roles in four, the network in five, the servers in six, and so on, to an edge cache and a reviewed, priced map in thirteen. The list says how to read every map from now on. A part keeps its place from the first frame to the last. A part drawn as a grey outline has not been built yet. A compared alternative is drawn beside the map, never inside it. And every number comes from one fixed example, labelled whenever it is assumed. Next, how A W S runs a request, starting with where in the world it runs.

Renting a server raises a question owning one never did: where is it? A W S answers with two boundaries, and both are about failure. The larger is the Region. A Region is a separate geographic area with its own copy of the services and its own endpoints, and the shop lives in one: E U west two, in London, close to its shoppers. Inside a Region are Availability Zones. E U west two has three, called a, b and c. Each zone is one or more data centres with their own power, cooling and network, far enough apart that a fire or a flood in one should not reach another, and close enough to be joined by fast private links. One detail in the list matters later: the names are per account. Your zone two a may be a different building from mine; the zone I D is the name that means the same place for everyone. The table on the right reads each failure against its boundary. A server fails, and the shop survives on another server. A data centre fails, and it survives on servers in other zones. A whole zone fails, drawn here as zone c in red, and the shop survives only if it has servers in the other two. A Region fails, and only a second Region helps, which is the last course's question. The second table makes this concrete with the shop's evening. The peak needs four servers. Put two in each of two zones and lose one zone, and two are left: not enough. Put two in each of three zones, six in all, and losing any zone still leaves four. That is the price of surviving a zone: capacity you hold in reserve, which the shop will pay for deliberately in Course six. Next, which services live in a zone, which in a Region, and which are global.

Every A W S resource lives at one of three scopes, and the scope decides what a failure takes with it. On the left are the global services, one for the whole account wherever you work: I A M, which holds identities and permissions; Route fifty three, the D N S service; CloudFront, the content delivery network; and Organizations, which groups accounts. In the middle are Regional resources, which live in one Region and spread themselves across its zones: an S three bucket, a DynamoDB table, an S Q S queue, a Lambda function, and a V P C, the shop's private network. On the right are zonal resources, which live in exactly one Availability Zone: an E C two instance, an E B S volume, which is the instance's disk, and a subnet, the slice of a V P C that sits in one zone. The table below says what each scope means when a zone fails. An I A M role is global, so you choose nothing, and a zone failure does not touch it. An S three bucket and a DynamoDB table are Regional: you choose the Region, and A W S keeps copies in several zones, so a zone failure loses no data. A subnet, an instance and a volume are zonal, and go down with their zone. A volume also attaches only to an instance in its own zone, which is why moving a disk between zones means a snapshot, as Course eight shows. The list on the right is how to choose a Region at all. Close to the shoppers, for lower latency. Where the data is allowed to live. The price, which differs by Region. And whether every service you need is offered there. The practical rule is simple: zonal resources are where you must spread for availability yourself; Regional services do much of that spreading for you. Next, how you actually ask A W S for any of this.

Everything you do in A W S, from creating a network to reading one file, is a call to an A P I. On the left are three ways to make that call. The console is a website, and every button in it sends the same A P I requests you could send yourself. The A W S C L I is a command-line program, where one command is one call, or a few. And an S D K, like boto three for Python, makes the calls from your own code. Whichever you use, the call becomes a signed H T T P S request to a service endpoint, here S three's endpoint in E U west two, and names one action, here HeadObject, which asks for an object's details without its contents. The service checks the signature, checks the permission, and only then acts. On the right is that same call twice. First as a C L I command: aws, the service, s three A P I, the action, head object, then the bucket and the key. Its parameters are checked against S three's own service model, the same model the C L I and the S D Ks are generated from. Below it, the same call in boto three: a client for S three, and head object with the same two parameters. The table says which client this course uses when. The console, to look, never to build, because clicks leave nothing that can be repeated or reviewed. The C L I, in the scripts that build the shop in Courses three to six. The S D K, in the app, the tools and the functions. And from Course seven, templates, which describe the result rather than the calls. The list says what every call has in common, whichever client sends it. It names one action on one resource, in one Region. It is signed by an identity, the subject of Course four. It can be recorded by CloudTrail, in Course twelve. And it counts against the account's quotas. Next, one of these requests taken apart.

Here is one request, taken apart, against the shop's map. The map is all grey except the buckets, because the shop builds nothing until Course three; for this one section a catalog bucket already exists, holding one product file. The terminal is emulated. Every command in this course runs the real A W S C L I and the real boto three, pointed at a local emulator rather than at A W S, and the pane's title says so whenever that is true. The first command is the head object call from the last section. The answer is the object's details, not its contents: its length, one thousand eight hundred and thirty four bytes; its type, J S O N; its E tag, a fingerprint of the content; and when it was last modified. The second command makes the same call through boto three, with a small hook that prints the request just before it is sent. The method is HEAD, and the U R L is S three's endpoint in E U west two, followed by the bucket and the key. Then comes the signature. The algorithm is A W S four H M A C S H A two fifty six, signature version four. The access key is the public half of a credential, here A W S's own documentation example. The scope ties the signature to one day, one Region and one service, so a captured request cannot be replayed elsewhere or later. The signed headers list what the signature covers, including the host and the time. And the signature itself is a keyed hash of the whole request, made with the secret half of the key, which never leaves your machine. Then the answer: status two hundred, and the same length. The table at the bottom names the six parts. An endpoint, an action, a resource, an identity, a scope and a signature are in every request you will ever send. Next, the names that resources go by: A R Ns.

A request named its bucket and its key. Policies, logs and other services need a name that is unique across every account and Region in the world, and that name is an A R N, an Amazon Resource Name. On the left is the A R N of the shop's order queue, split into its six fields, read in pairs from the top. Every A R N starts with the letters arn. Then the partition, a w s for the ordinary commercial Regions. Then the service, S Q S. Then the Region, E U west two. Then the account, one one one one, two two two two, three three three three. And last, the resource, the queue called order events. The table on the right shows the whole queue A R N in its first row, then more of the shop's resources, and they are not all the same shape. The order queue has every field. The app's I A M role has no Region, because I A M is global, so that field is simply empty. The catalog bucket has neither a Region nor an account, because bucket names are already unique worldwide. One product file is the bucket's A R N, a slash, and the object's key. Every product file is the same with a star in place of the file name, which is how a policy will say all of these at once. And a server is an E C two instance A R N, with its Region, its account and its instance I D. The list says how to read one. An empty field means the service does not need it. I A M has no Region. Bucket names need no Region and no account. A star matches many resources. And in Course four the shop's policies will name exactly what they allow by A R N, so getting one wrong grants the wrong thing, or nothing at all. Next, the last idea before the project starts: what these resources cost, and which ones keep costing when you think you have stopped them.

Every resource has a meter, and the meters do not all stop together. The table on the left lists the ones the shop will use, at this course's hypothetical rates: invented, realistic numbers, labelled whenever they appear, because real prices change and differ by Region. An E C two instance bills by the hour while it runs, at four cents an hour, and nothing while it is stopped. Its E B S volume bills for every gigabyte you have provisioned, eight cents a gigabyte-month, whether the instance is running, stopped, or the volume is not attached at all. A public I P version four address bills half a cent an hour for as long as you hold it. A snapshot bills five cents a gigabyte-month for as long as it is kept. S three bills for what it stores, plus a charge per request. Data leaving A W S for the internet bills by the gigabyte, and data coming in is free. The table on the right is the shop's development account for one month. Running all month, the instance costs twenty nine dollars twenty. The volume adds one sixty, the address three sixty five, a snapshot one dollar, and thirty three gigabytes in S three seventy six cents: thirty six dollars twenty one. Stop the instance, and only its line goes to zero. The month still costs seven dollars and one cent, because stopping is not deleting, and everything that was provisioned is still there. The list gives the three shapes every bill takes: per hour for things that exist, like servers, addresses and gateways; per gigabyte for storage and for data leaving; and per request for calls to services like S three, queues and functions. Course three turns this into the shop's own cost ledger and its cleanup script, from the first resource it creates. Next, the project itself.

From here on, the shop is a real project on disk, called shop on A W S, and this is the layout every lesson uses. On the left is the project as an editor shows it, finished, as it will be at the end of the course. In the centre, where code will normally be, is what each part is for and the course that builds it. Two small things come first, in this course: env dot sh, which sets the Region and says where commands go, and a Python environment with boto three. Then infra, the A W S C L I scripts that build the shop's resources one command at a time, from this course to Course six. Policies holds every permission as J S O N, from Course four. App is the order A P I itself, and later its container image. Templates holds the same resources again, but declared rather than scripted, from Course seven, and pipeline builds the app once and deploys it to two accounts. Catalog and d b hold the product data and the orders schema. Functions and workflow are the asynchronous checkout in Course ten. Jobs exports and reports on sales in Course eleven. Ops holds the runbooks for incidents and restores in Course twelve. Tools holds the course's calculations, from costs to capacity. And docs holds the decision record that closes the course. On the right is how to read every lesson. The left panel is the project, and a file marked new is one this lesson adds. The centre shows the open file with this lesson's lines highlighted, and beneath it the terminal, exactly as it ran. A terminal marked emulated ran against a local emulator rather than A W S, which this course explains in a moment. And three dots with a line count folds away what the lesson does not need. Next, the account itself, and the one identity in it that can do anything.

Every A W S resource belongs to an account, and the shop's development work happens in one: account four four four four, five five five five, six six six six. On the left are the identities inside it. At the top, in red, is the root user: the email address and password that opened the account. Root can do anything in the account, and no I A M policy can limit it, which is exactly why it is dangerous. Below are the identities that should do the work. The shop's people, alex and sam, sign in through I A M Identity Center, and the app itself will act through an I A M role called OrderApi. Both arrive in Course four. The table lists the few jobs that genuinely need root: changing the account's email, name or root password; closing the account; restoring access when no administrator can sign in any more; and a handful of billing and tax settings. Everything else should be done by someone else. The list on the right is how to lock it away. Turn on multi-factor authentication for root before you do anything else in a new account, so a stolen password is not enough. Never create access keys for root, because a key in a script or on a laptop would be a permanent copy of the most powerful credential you own. Sign in as root only for the jobs in the table. Do everyday work through Identity Center instead. And in an organization, which Course four builds, member accounts can have no root password at all, with the few root tasks run centrally. The mistake to avoid is the convenient one: using root because it never says access denied. That convenience is the risk. Next, a first session that is not root: a person signing in with temporary credentials.

Here is how alex, the shop's developer, starts work, with the map still nearly empty. The terminal shows the real A W S C L I, not the emulator, and its first command prints alex's configuration file. It holds one profile, shop dev, that names the development account, four four four four, five five five five, six six six six, and a permission set called ShopDeveloper, in E U west two. The profile points at an S S O session called shop, which names the shop's access portal. There is no key in this file. The second command asks the simplest question there is: who am I? It fails before any request is sent, because there is no S S O token yet: alex has not logged in. The table is what aws s s o login does, from A W S's documentation, because a sign-in needs a browser and a real Identity Center, and the emulator has neither. A browser opens the shop's portal. Alex signs in, with M F A, and approves the C L I. The C L I caches a token in the home folder. From then on, each command trades that token for credentials of the ShopDeveloper role in the dev account. And those credentials expire, so no long-lived key ever sits on the laptop. Underneath is what the same who am I question returns after login. Its shape is checked against S T S's own model, and its values are invented. The account is the dev account. The A R N is an assumed role: an Identity Center role named after the permission set, with a random suffix, and the session is named alex. That one line answers who, in which account, with which permissions. It is the first thing to run when anything is denied. Next, the emulator this course runs its commands against, and why.

This course has no A W S account behind it, and you do not need one to follow it. Instead, every command runs against an emulator: a local server called moto that answers the same A P I calls A W S does. The file open in the editor, env dot sh, is the whole switch. Line two sets the Region, E U west two, for every command in the project. Lines six to eight are the emulator: an endpoint U R L on localhost, and a key pair that the emulator accepts and that is, in fact, A W S's own documentation example. The comment says how to run the same scripts against A W S itself: delete those three lines, and use the shop dev profile from the last section instead. Nothing else in the project changes. In the terminal, sourcing the file and asking who am I now succeeds. The emulator answers in the dev account, four four four four, five five five five, six six six six, as a placeholder user called moto, because it has no Identity Center. Listing buckets returns an empty list: a brand new account. The table on the right is the honest boundary. The emulator shows A P I answers and errors, resources and their state, I A M policy decisions, and the behaviour of queues, conditional writes and retries. It cannot show packets crossing a network, software running on a server, organization guardrails and cross-account checks, or failover, edge caching and quotas. The list is how the course handles that. The C L I and boto three are real; only the endpoint changes. Every pane run against the emulator says emulated in its title. Whatever the emulator cannot show is shown by a small model, run for real, or by cited documentation, and the frame says which. Next, the shop's first real resource.

The shop's first resource is the catalog bucket, and on the map the buckets are now lit. The script on the right, infra slash zero one bucket, builds it. Line three makes the script stop at the first error, which matters in a moment. Line five asks who am I and keeps only the account number, and line six builds the bucket's name from it: shop catalog, then the account, because bucket names are global and an account number makes one unlikely to be taken. Lines eight and nine create the bucket in E U west two. Lines eleven and twelve tag it: app shop, environment dev, owner alex. Tags cost nothing and answer the question every bill eventually asks, which is whose is this. Line thirteen uploads the first product file, and prints its E tag. In the terminal, the first run creates shop catalog four four four four, five five five five, six six six six, and prints the E tag. Listing the bucket shows one object: products slash p dash one thousand and one dot json, one thousand eight hundred and thirty four bytes, the file Course two asked about. Then the script runs a second time, and fails. The bucket already exists and belongs to this account, and outside the U S east one Region, S three answers create bucket on such a bucket with an error, BucketAlreadyOwnedByYou. Because of line three, the script stops right there instead of carrying on half done. The list draws the lesson. A script records what to do, not what should exist, so running it twice is a different request from running it once. Every C L I script in this course has this property, and Course seven replaces them with templates that describe the result instead. Next, what the account costs, and how to remove what we made.

Every resource the shop creates is a cost from that moment, so this course ends with two new files: one that prices the account, and one that removes what infra built. The editor shows tools slash cost ledger. Lines two and three are the course's hypothetical rate card, the same invented rates as before. The ledger lists what the dev account will hold once it has a server: the server itself for seven hundred and thirty hours, its twenty gigabyte volume, a public address, a twenty gigabyte snapshot, and thirty three gigabytes of catalog in S three. Each entry says whether it is still billed when the server is stopped. Line sixteen adds an item to the stopped total only when it is. The terminal shows the result. Running all month costs thirty six dollars twenty one. Stopped, it is still seven dollars and one cent, because only the server's own hours stop. Then the new teardown script runs, and the table on the right gives its steps, newest resource first. It removes every object, because a bucket must be empty before it can be deleted, then deletes the bucket, and the last command checks by listing buckets and finding none. The list below it is the habit this course keeps. A budget, in A W S Budgets, is an alarm, not a cap: it emails when actual or forecast cost crosses a line you set, and it stops nothing unless you configure an action to do so. Tags, like app, env and owner, are what let a bill say whose cost is whose. And cleanup is a script, kept beside the scripts that create things, and grown with them every time a new resource appears. That completes the start: a project, a profile, an emulator, a first resource, a price, and a way back to nothing. Next course, who is allowed to do any of this.

Every request A W S receives is signed by a principal, and this course decides who those principals are. On the map, I A M roles now light up. The first table lists the kinds of principal. A person, like alex or sam, signs in to I A M Identity Center and receives credentials for a role. A workload, like the shop's app servers, assumes a role of its own, OrderApi. An A W S service, like E C two, is named in a role's trust policy so that it may assume the role on a workload's behalf. Root, from the last course, is locked away. And an I A M user with a long-lived access key is a kind of principal the shop does not use at all, because a key that never expires is a key that eventually leaks. The second table is how the shop's people are assigned. Identity Center groups people, and assigns a group to an account with a permission set, which is a template for a role. Developers, which is alex, get ShopDeveloper in the dev account and only ShopReadOnly in production. Operators, which is sam, get ShopOperator in production, and it is sam's session that runs the scripts that build production until Course seven hands that job to a pipeline. The list separates two words that are easy to blur. Authentication proves who you are, with a password and M F A, at the identity source. Federation turns that proof into temporary credentials for a role. Authorisation then decides what those credentials may do, by evaluating the role's policies on every single request. And a permission set becomes one real role in each account it is assigned to, which is the A W S reserved S S O role you saw in the last course's caller identity. Next, the accounts themselves, and why production and development are not the same account.

The shop does not live in one account. It lives in an organization, and on the map the accounts now light up beside the roles. The tree on the right is that organization, managed with A W S Organizations. At its root is the management account, one two three four five six seven eight nine zero one two. Under the root are organisational units, or O Us, which are folders for accounts. The Security O U holds the audit account, seven seven seven seven, eight eight eight eight, nine nine nine nine. The Workloads O U holds two more O Us, Prod and Dev, and in each is one account: production, one one one one, two two two two, three three three three, which the map describes, and development, four four four four, five five five five, six six six six, where Course three began. The table says why these are separate accounts rather than separate folders in one. An account is the strongest boundary A W S has. Resources in it are its own, so a development script cannot touch production. I A M is per account, so an administrator in development is nobody in production unless deliberately given access. Quotas are per account, so a load test in development cannot use up production's limits. The bill is per account by default, so cost follows the boundary. And the blast radius of a leaked development key is development. The list describes the management account's special job. It creates accounts and O Us and pays the consolidated bill, and it runs no workloads, partly because the guardrails in the last section of this course never apply to it. The audit account owns the logs that record what everyone did, so the people being audited cannot edit the record. Next, the app's own identity: a role for OrderApi, and the policy that says who may use it.

The app servers need to read products and send order events, and they must do it without a key stored on disk. The answer is a role, and a role is two documents. The file open in the editor is the first: the trust policy, in the policies folder. It has one statement, called AppServersOnly. Its effect is allow, its action is s t s assume role, and its principal is the E C two service. In words: the only thing allowed to become this role is E C two, acting for a server. Not alex, not sam, not another account. In the terminal, the new script infra zero four roles creates the role from that document and prints its A R N, in the production account. It then creates an instance profile with the same name and puts the role inside it, because an instance profile is the container E C two uses to hand a role to a server. The last command reads the trust policy back from I A M, and the principal is the E C two service, as written. The table on the right separates the two questions a role answers. The trust policy asks, who may be me, and names a principal. The permissions policy asks, what may I do, and names actions and resources. For OrderApi, the answer to the first is E C two only. The answer to the second does not exist yet, which the list makes explicit. Trust alone grants nothing. Right now OrderApi can be assumed by a server, and the server can then do nothing at all, because nothing allows anything. That is the right default, and the next two sections build on it: first what assuming the role produces, then the permissions. Next, assuming the role, and the credentials it hands back.

Assuming a role is one call to S T S, the security token service, and its answer is a set of temporary credentials. In the terminal, the call is made by hand, naming the OrderApi role and a session called app dash b, after the server it stands for. The answer, cut to two fields, is an access key I D starting with A S I A, which marks a temporary key, and an expiry exactly one hour after the emulator's clock, the default duration. The full answer also carries a secret and a session token. The second command uses a profile that assumes the role automatically, and asks who am I. The answer is an assumed role: OrderApi, session app b, in the production account. That A R N is what every request from the server will be signed as, and what every log will record. The table compares what a server holds with and without a role. An I A M user's key starts A K I A, lives until someone rotates it, and if it leaks, it works until someone notices. A role session starts A S I A, carries a session token, lives an hour and is refreshed, and if it leaks, it stops working at its expiry. The list is the honest part. The emulator ran this with I A M enforcement off, so it did not check the trust policy from the last section. On A W S, this exact call, made by a person, is refused, because only E C two may assume OrderApi. On a real server, E C two makes this call itself, through the instance profile, and hands the credentials to the server through its instance metadata service, refreshing them before they expire. The application code never sees a key at all; the S D K finds the credentials. Next, what the role is allowed to do.

The second document is the permissions policy, open in the editor: OrderApiAccess. It has three statements, and each one answers the same four questions. ReadProducts allows the action s three get object, on every object whose key starts with products slash in the catalog bucket. That is read, never write. ListProducts, highlighted, allows s three list bucket. Its resource is the bucket itself, not the objects in it, because listing is an action on the bucket. And it has a condition: the listing may only ask for keys that start with products slash, so the app can browse products but not anything else stored in the same bucket. SendOrderEvents allows s q s send message on one queue, order events, in the production account. Send, but not receive, and not delete: another component will consume those events. In the terminal, put role policy attaches this document to OrderApi as an inline policy, and the same line is now the last line of infra zero four roles, so a rebuild includes it. Reading it back lists the three statements: their I Ds, their effect, which is allow for all three, and their action. The table on the right is the four questions. Effect: allow or deny. Action: which A P I calls. Resource: on which A R Ns. And condition: only when, which is optional. The list reads the policy as least privilege, one line at a time. Read products, never write them. List the bucket, but only under products. Send to one queue, not receive from it. And notice that list bucket names the bucket while get object names objects; giving one A R N where the other is expected is the most common reason a policy that looks right allows nothing. Next, a request that is denied, and exactly why.

Some products are drafts, kept under products slash drafts, and the app must never serve them. The policy in the editor has a fourth statement for that, DenyDrafts, highlighted in red: deny get object on anything under products slash drafts. In the terminal, a probe script makes the app's requests as OrderApi, and this time the emulator enforces I A M on every request. The first line confirms the identity: the assumed role OrderApi, session app b. Then five requests. Reading product one thousand and one is allowed. Reading a draft is denied. Reading an order is denied. Overwriting a product is denied. And sending an order event is allowed. The table on the right says what decided each one, and the list gives the order I A M evaluates in. It starts from deny: nothing is allowed unless something allows it. Then any explicit deny ends the evaluation, whatever else allows. The draft is under products slash star, so ReadProducts allows it, but DenyDrafts denies it explicitly, and the explicit deny wins. The order and the overwrite are different: nothing denies them, but nothing allows them either, so they stay at the default. That is an implicit deny. Both look the same to the caller, access denied, but they are fixed in opposite ways: an implicit deny needs an allow added, while an explicit deny means someone decided this must not happen, and adding an allow changes nothing. The product read and the event send are allowed by ReadProducts and SendOrderEvents. The last item in the list is a limit of the emulator. Listing orders slash is denied on A W S by ListProducts' condition, but the emulator does not evaluate conditions, so that case is stated from A W S's documentation rather than shown. Next, policies attached to resources, and requests from another account.

So far every policy was attached to an identity. Some services also accept a policy attached to the resource itself, and S three's bucket policy is the shop's first. The shop's sales reports live in a bucket in production, shop reports, and the auditor, working from the audit account, must be able to read them. The file in the editor is the bucket policy. Its one statement, AuditorReads, allows get object and list bucket, on the bucket and on everything in it. What makes it a resource policy is the principal: it names who is allowed, here the role Auditor in account seven seven seven seven, eight eight eight eight, nine nine nine nine. In the terminal, put bucket policy attaches it to the bucket, and get bucket policy status confirms the bucket is not public, because the principal is one named role rather than a star. The table on the right is the rule that makes this work, and it differs by where the caller comes from. Within one account, an allow in either the caller's identity policy or the resource's policy is enough. Across accounts, both must allow. The bucket policy here is production saying the Auditor may come in. The second new file, auditor reads, is the identity policy in the audit account, the audit account saying the Auditor may go out and read this bucket. The list spells out the consequence: remove either one, and the read is denied. That two-sided rule is what keeps one account from granting itself access to another's data. The emulator does not model cross-account evaluation, so the both-sides rule here is A W S's documented behaviour. Next, guardrails that cap what any policy can grant, and who owns the audit trail.

Every policy so far granted something. The last kind removes, and it applies to whole groups of accounts at once. The file in the editor is a service control policy, or S C P, called StayInLondon. Its one statement denies every action, with a set of exceptions, whenever the requested Region is not E U west two. The exceptions are in NotAction: I A M, Organizations, S T S, Route fifty three, CloudFront, budgets and support, global services whose calls do not belong to E U west two, and which would break if they were denied. In the terminal, a script run in the management account finds the organization's root, finds the Workloads O U, creates the policy, attaches it to the O U, and lists where it is attached: the Workloads organisational unit. From now on, nobody in production or development, not alex, not sam, not even an account administrator, can create anything outside London. The table sorts the four policy kinds. Identity policies grant a principal. Resource policies grant on a resource. An S C P caps what principals in an O U can do. And a resource control policy, an R C P, caps what can be done to resources in an O U, for example that a bucket can only be reached from inside the organization. The list makes the essential point first: an S C P grants nothing. A request still needs an allow from an identity or resource policy; the S C P can only remove permissions that would otherwise be granted. NotAction keeps the global services working. The audit account is the organization's delegated administrator for the logs, so the record of who did what is owned outside the accounts it describes. And the emulator only stores and attaches the S C P; enforcing it is A W S's job, as documented. Next course, the network the shop's requests travel.

Before the shop has a network, it needs an address plan, and this course starts with one small Python file. A private network's addresses are written in C I D R notation: an address, a slash, and a number of fixed bits. The editor shows tools slash c i d r plan. Line four takes the shop's whole range, ten dot twenty dot zero dot zero slash sixteen. Sixteen fixed bits leave sixteen free, so the terminal's first line says it holds sixty five thousand five hundred and thirty six addresses. Lines seven to twelve cut it into nine slash twenty four subnets, one for each of three tiers in each of three Availability Zones. Public uses third numbers zero to two, app ten to twelve, and data twenty to twenty two, so a glance at an address says its tier. Line ten checks that every subnet sits inside the V P C's range. Line twelve is the A W S detail: a slash twenty four has two hundred and fifty six addresses, but A W S keeps five in every subnet, for the network address, the V P C's router, D N S, a reserved one and the last address, so each subnet has two hundred and fifty one usable. The last check places one real address, ten dot twenty dot eleven dot thirty seven, the app server in zone b, inside app b. This run is plain Python on the laptop: nothing here touched the emulator, and the terminal's title says so. On the right are the ports the shop uses: four four three for H T T P S from shoppers, eight zero eight zero for the app behind the load balancer, five four three two for PostgreSQL, and fifty three for D N S. The list adds the one rule that is hard to fix later. Ranges that may ever connect must not overlap, which is why development uses ten dot thirty. Next, the V P C itself, built across three zones.

Now the plan becomes a network, inside the V P C box on the map. The script on the right, infra zero five network, does it in two moves. Line five creates the V P C with the shop's range and names it shop prod. A V P C belongs to a Region, so it spans all three zones. Lines eleven and twelve are a small function that creates one subnet, in one zone, with one range and a name. A subnet, unlike its V P C, lives in exactly one zone. The function is called nine times, once per row of the plan from the last section. The terminal shows the result: the V P C's I D, then nine subnet I Ds, each with its name, its zone and its range. Every I D here is the emulator's, and stays the same on every replay. The table says what each tier is for, which is the real design decision. The public tier holds what must be reachable from the internet, the load balancer, and the NAT gateway that lets private servers reach out. The app tier holds the app servers. Each server gets a network interface, an E N I, with a private address from its subnet, like ten dot twenty dot eleven dot thirty seven in app b, and the app tier is reachable from the load balancer only. The data tier holds the orders database, reachable from the app servers only. Spreading every tier over three zones is what lets the shop lose a zone, as Course two showed, and keep serving. Nothing yet makes any of these subnets public or private. That is decided not by the subnet but by its route table. Next, route tables, and how a packet's route is chosen.

A route table decides where a packet leaving a subnet goes next. In the terminal, infra zero five routes creates an internet gateway, igw shop, attaches it to the V P C, and creates a route table, r t public. That table gets a route for zero dot zero dot zero dot zero slash zero, which means every address, pointing at the internet gateway, and it is associated with the three public subnets. The script prints the table's I D and its routes: local, and the default route via the gateway. The table below lists them. The local route, for the whole V P C range, is in every route table, and cannot be removed. Then two questions, asked by a small tool, route pick, which reads the real route table from the emulator and picks a route the way the V P C router does. From public a to ten dot twenty dot eleven dot thirty seven, the app server: two routes contain that address, the local slash sixteen and the default slash zero, and the longest prefix wins, so the packet stays local. From public a to one nine eight dot fifty one dot one hundred dot seven, the payments provider: only the default route contains it, so it leaves through the internet gateway. The list states the rule and one common confusion. Every route that contains the destination is a candidate, and the most specific, the longest prefix, wins. The local route always exists. And a public subnet is public only because its route table reaches an internet gateway; a server in it still needs a public address and an open security group before anyone can reach it. Next, the app subnets, which have no route out at all yet.

The app servers must call the payments A P I, at one nine eight dot fifty one dot one hundred dot seven, but they live in a private subnet. The terminal starts with that call's route from app a, and the answer is no route: app a has no table of its own, so it uses the V P C's main table, which knows only the local range, and the packet is dropped. On a real server this is the classic symptom: the payment call times out rather than failing with a clear error. The fix is infra zero five egress. It allocates an elastic I P address, creates a NAT gateway called nat a in the public subnet public a, waits for it to be available, and creates r t app a, with a default route pointing at the NAT gateway, for the app a subnet. Asked again, route pick finds the default route via the NAT gateway. The table says who can start a connection, and this is the point of a private subnet. From the internet to the load balancer in a public subnet: yes, through the internet gateway. From the internet to a server in app a: no, there is no route in. From a server in app a to the payments A P I: yes, through the NAT gateway and then the internet gateway. And from the payments A P I back to the server, starting a new connection: no, a NAT gateway only carries connections that started inside, plus their replies. The list is about cost and failure. A NAT gateway lives in one zone, so if zone a fails, servers in b and c lose the internet too. Production therefore runs one per zone: three, at five cents an hour each on the hypothetical rate card, is one hundred and nine dollars fifty a month before any data, and Course thirteen finds that is the shop's largest single line. Next, the filters that decide which connections are accepted at all.

Routes decide where a packet can go; filters decide whether it is accepted when it arrives. The shop's filters are security groups, and the terminal runs infra zero five filters, which creates three and prints their I Ds, then lists each group with the port it allows. The first table is the design: a chain. s g a l b admits T C P four four three from anywhere, because shoppers come from anywhere. s g app admits T C P eight zero eight zero, but only from members of s g a l b: the source is not an address range but another security group. And s g d b admits T C P five four three two, PostgreSQL, only from members of s g app. Each tier admits only the tier before it. Because sources are groups rather than addresses, the rule keeps working when servers are replaced and their addresses change, which Course six does constantly. The second table compares security groups with the other filter a V P C offers, the network A C L. A security group is attached to a network interface, holds only allow rules, and is stateful: a reply to an allowed request is let back out automatically. A network A C L is attached to a subnet, holds numbered allow and deny rules, and is stateless: return traffic must be allowed explicitly, in the other direction, including the high-numbered ports replies use. Its source can only be an address range, never a group. The shop leaves its network A C Ls at the default, which allows everything, and does its filtering with security groups. A network A C L earns its place when you need a deny, such as blocking one address range from a whole subnet. Next, the name shoppers type: shop dot example dot com.

Shoppers type shop dot example dot com, not an address, and on the map Route fifty three now lights up. The file at the top right is the change the shop asks Route fifty three to make. It is an upsert, meaning create or replace, of an A record for shop dot example dot com. Instead of addresses, it holds an alias target: the load balancer's D N S name in E U west two, and the hosted zone that A W S uses for application load balancers in that Region. Evaluate target health is true, so Route fifty three can stop answering with an unhealthy target. In the terminal, infra zero five d n s creates the hosted zone for example dot com, applies the change, whose status comes back in sync, and lists the A records: shop dot example dot com, aliased to the load balancer. The table follows one lookup. The shopper's resolver asks the dot com servers who holds example dot com, and is sent to Route fifty three's name servers for the zone. Route fifty three answers the alias with the load balancer's current addresses, which can change as the load balancer scales, and an alias always follows them, which a fixed address could not. The shopper then connects to one of those addresses on port four four three. The list names the routing policies beyond simple. Weighted splits answers by percentage, which Course thirteen uses to move traffic during a migration. Failover answers with a standby when a health check fails. Latency answers with the Region nearest the shopper. Next, the connection that follows the lookup, and where it is encrypted.

Reaching the shop is one question; whether anyone on the way can read the traffic is another, and this frame answers it hop by hop. The first table follows a request. From the shopper to the load balancer, the connection is H T T P S, T L S version one point three, using a certificate for shop dot example dot com from A W S Certificate Manager, so nobody on the way can read it. From the load balancer to an app server, inside the V P C, the shop sends plain H T T P on port eight zero eight zero, with no certificate: anything on that internal path could read it. From the app to the orders database, the PostgreSQL connection uses T L S with the R D S certificate authority, which Course nine sets up. The second table is the listener that does the first hop. It listens on four four three, uses the A C M certificate, which must be requested in the load balancer's own Region, E U west two, and is validated by a D N S record in example dot com, so A C M can renew it automatically before it expires. Its security policy, E L B security policy T L S thirteen, allows only T L S one point two and one point three. The list is what to take away. Encryption ends where the certificate is, here at the load balancer, so the load balancer sees the request in clear. Reaching a server tells you nothing about whether the path to it was encrypted; reachability is routing and filtering, encryption is a separate decision. A load balancer's certificate lives in its own Region, while CloudFront, in Course thirteen, needs its certificate in U S east one. And encrypting the last hop too is possible, at the cost of a certificate on every server. Next, the load balancer itself, and how it decides a server is healthy.

The load balancer now lights up on the map. In the terminal, infra zero five l b creates two things. First a target group, shop app: the set of servers the load balancer may send to, and how it checks them. Then the load balancer itself, shop a l b, an application load balancer across the three public subnets, behind the s g a l b security group. The table holds the target group's settings. It sends H T T P to port eight zero eight zero. It checks every target by asking for slash health every ten seconds, and the app answers two hundred when it is ready. Two failures in a row mark a target unhealthy; three successes mark it healthy again. The second half of the terminal is a model, not A W S: health timeline, a small program that plays those settings forward for one server, app three, which stops answering at zero seconds and recovers at sixty. Checks run at five seconds, fifteen, twenty five and so on. The first failed check is not enough; at fifteen seconds the second is, and app three is marked unhealthy, so the load balancer stops sending it requests. It keeps checking. From sixty five seconds app three answers again, and after the third success, at eighty five seconds, it is healthy and back in service. The last two lines are the cost of losing it. At the evening's five hundred and sixty requests a second, six servers carry ninety three each; with app three out, the other five carry one hundred and twelve, still under the one hundred and fifty one server can take, which is why the shop runs six. For those fifteen seconds before it was marked down, though, some requests still went to app three and failed. Health checks limit the damage; they do not prevent it. Next, private paths that leave the V P C without crossing the internet.

Not every connection out of the V P C should go through the NAT gateway and the internet. On the left are the shop's private paths. The app servers reach S three through a gateway endpoint: a target in the route table, for S three's address ranges, so catalog reads stay on A W S's network and skip the NAT gateway and its per gigabyte charge. Beyond the V P C are three other destinations: S three in the same Region, the development V P C at ten dot thirty, and, for a company that had one, an office or a data centre. The table compares the ways to reach them. A gateway endpoint joins a V P C to S three or DynamoDB, with no NAT and no hourly charge. An interface endpoint joins a V P C to most other services, through a network interface in your subnets, and costs per hour in each zone. Peering joins two V P Cs one to one; it is not transitive, so if A peers with B and B with C, A still cannot reach C, and the two ranges must not overlap, which is the reason for the address plan at the start of this course. A Transit Gateway is a hub that routes between many V P Cs and networks. A site to site V P N joins a site over the internet, encrypted, and is quick to set up. And Direct Connect is a dedicated line with steady bandwidth, which is private but not encrypted by default, so you add encryption on top. The list says what the shop uses. An S three gateway endpoint for the catalog. A peering connection, p c x dev, to the development V P C, so r t app a has a route for ten dot thirty slash sixteen through it. And no V P N or Direct Connect, because the shop has no office network to join. That completes the network: a request can now find the shop, reach it securely, and be filtered all the way in. Next course, the servers that answer it.

Before choosing where the app runs, here is the app. The editor shows app slash server dot p y, version one of the order A P I, built on Python's standard library H T T P server. Line fourteen answers slash health with two hundred, the check the load balancer from the last course will make. Lines fifteen to twenty one answer a product request: they turn slash products slash p dash one thousand and one into the key products slash p dash one thousand and one dot json, read that object from the catalog bucket through boto three, and return it, or a four oh four if there is no such product. Nothing in the file is a key or a password: boto three finds its credentials the way the C L I did, which on a server will be the OrderApi role. In the terminal, the server starts in the background on port eight zero eight zero, on the laptop. The first request asks for product one thousand and one, and jq keeps four fields: its I D, its name, a ceramic pour over coffee dripper, its price, twelve pounds, and its stock, forty. The catalog bucket here is the emulator's, while the server and curl are real. A product that does not exist returns four oh four. The health check returns status ok. Stopping the server shows its log: one line per request, with the status. On the right, the table lists what the app answers, and the list says why it is shaped this way. Products come from S three, so any server can answer any request, which is what the rest of this course depends on. There is no key in the code. It listens on eight zero eight zero, the one port s g app admits from the load balancer. And orders and carts arrive later, deliberately. Next, the four places this app could run on A W S.

The order A P I could run on A W S in four different ways, and on the left is one card for each. E C two gives virtual machines: you choose the instance, the operating system and its patching, and it runs anything for as long as you like. E C S on Fargate runs containers with no servers to see: you supply an image and a size, and A W S runs the hosts underneath. Lambda runs a function per request: you supply a handler, each call may last up to fifteen minutes, and a call that finds no warm environment pays a cold start. E K S is managed Kubernetes: A W S runs the control plane, and you run Kubernetes workloads and the nodes beneath them. The table compares them for this app. Control is greatest on E C two and least on Lambda. Operational work follows control: on E C two you own the operating system, patches and scaling; on Fargate, mostly just the image; on Lambda, the least; on E K S, a cluster and its nodes. Latency is steady for the three that keep processes running, while Lambda has occasional cold starts. And each bills differently: E C two per second while running, Fargate per second per task, Lambda per request and duration, E K S per cluster hour plus its nodes. The list matches the choice to the app. The order A P I is a long running H T T P server with steady traffic, which fits E C two or Fargate. This course builds it first on E C two, in sections three to six, because there every layer is visible: the image, the boot, the scaling. Then section seven runs the same app as a Fargate task. Lambda arrives for the checkout in Course ten, E K S is weighed in section eight, and Course thirteen compares all three for the whole platform. Next, the first server, from a template.

The app servers now light up on the map, and every one of them starts from the same template. The script on the right, infra zero six template, builds it. Lines five and six look up the latest Amazon Linux image for Graviton, from a public parameter A W S keeps, rather than hard-coding an image I D that goes out of date. Then it creates a launch template called order api, whose data names that image, the instance type m seven g large, the OrderApi instance profile from Course four, the s g app security group, and, on line sixteen, metadata options with H T T P tokens required. That last setting enforces I M D S version two: the server's metadata, including its role credentials, can only be read with a session token, which blocks a whole class of attacks that trick a server into fetching its own credentials. In the terminal, the template is version one. Reading it back shows the instance type and that tokens are required. Then one server is launched from the template into app b, and described: its I D, running, in E U west two b. Stopping it moves it from running to stopping, and terminating it from stopped to shutting down. The table is that lifecycle. Pending to running, and billed from running. Stopping to stopped, with no instance hours but the disk kept and still billed. Shutting down to terminated, with the disk deleted by default. Two emulator details are worth knowing. It reports a new instance as running at once, where A W S passes through pending first. And it does not copy the template's metadata options onto the instance, which is why the frame reads the template back instead. Production is on a later version of this template, and every change will be a new version. Next, what an m seven g large is, and three ways to pay for it.

An instance type's name is a code, and the table on the right reads m seven g large. M is the family, general purpose, balanced between processor and memory. Seven is the generation. G means Graviton, A W S's Arm processor, usually the best price for performance when the software runs on Arm, as Python does. And large is the size: two virtual C P Us and eight gibibytes of memory. Then the question of how to pay, which the editor answers for one month. Line two is the hypothetical rate card for this type: four cents an hour on demand, two point eight cents with a one year commitment, and one point six cents on Spot. The fleet on lines six to eight is the shop's real shape. Three servers run all day, every day, as the baseline: certain use, so it is bought with a commitment. Three more run six hours each evening for the peak, bought on demand because they come and go. And two image worker servers run four hours a night, bought on Spot. The terminal is plain Python on the laptop. The baseline is two thousand one hundred and sixty server hours for sixty dollars forty eight. The evening peak is five hundred and forty hours for twenty one sixty. The image workers are two hundred and forty hours for three eighty four. The month is eighty five dollars ninety two, against one hundred and seventeen sixty if everything were on demand. The list says what each buys and costs. On demand promises nothing and pays the full rate. A commitment promises a year of use and pays less. Spot uses spare capacity at a deep discount, but A W S can take it back with two minutes' notice, so Spot suits work that can stop and resume, like resizing images, and never the baseline that serves shoppers. Next, what happens on a server's first boot, and how to reach it without S S H.

A server launched from the template has an operating system and nothing else. The file in the editor, app slash user data dot s h, is what turns it into an app server, and it runs once, as root, on the server's first boot. Lines six and seven install pip and boto three. Line eight copies the release, order api one point four point two, from the releases bucket, using the server's OrderApi role. Line nine unpacks it. Line ten creates a system user for the app, and the lines after that write a service definition, so the operating system starts the app, restarts it if it crashes, and starts it again after a reboot. Line nineteen enables and starts it. In the terminal, bash checks the script's syntax, which it passes. Then a new template version is created from version one, with this script added as user data, base sixty four encoded, and the new version is number two. The last command uses Systems Manager Run Command to apply security updates on every server tagged app order api. It returns a command I D. The emulator records the command and runs nothing, so all that is shown is that the call was accepted. The table is why Systems Manager matters. Running a command on many servers is Run Command. A shell on one server is Session Manager. Patching on a schedule is Patch Manager. And none of them needs an inbound port or an S S H key: the S S M agent on the server connects out, using the server's role, and every session can be logged. The list is the other half of the shared responsibility model from Course one: on E C two, the operating system and its patches, the Python runtime, and starting, restarting and logging the app are all still the shop's job. Next, a group of these servers that grows and shrinks on its own.

One server is a single point of failure, and the shop's day needs three in the morning and six in the evening. An Auto Scaling group handles both. The script on the right, infra zero six scaling, creates the group order api from the latest template version, with a minimum of three, a maximum of nine and three to start, across the three app subnets, one in each zone, and attached to the shop app target group. Health check type E L B means the group replaces any server the load balancer marks unhealthy, after a grace period of one hundred and twenty seconds for it to boot. The last command adds a scheduled action, evening peak, that raises the minimum to six at seventeen forty five every day, London time. In the terminal, the group reports a minimum of three, desired three, maximum nine, and three instances. The scheduled action is evening peak, at seventeen forty five, Europe London, minimum six. The last lines are a model, surge dot p y, not A W S. It plays the evening forward minute by minute, with demand jumping from two hundred and forty to five hundred and sixty requests a second at eighteen hundred, and new servers taking five minutes to come into service. Scaling only in reaction to load, three servers carry four hundred and fifty, so the shop is one hundred and ten requests a second short from eighteen hundred to eighteen oh four, while new servers boot. With the schedule, six are in service before the surge, and the shop is never short. The list says what the group does on its own. On A W S it spreads the minimum of three, one per zone; the emulator placed all three in zone a, which is why the frame shows the group's sizes instead. It replaces unhealthy servers. And it scales ahead of a surge you can predict, rather than behind it. Next, the same app, in a container.

The user data script from section five builds a server in minutes, every time a server starts. A container image does that work once, at build time, and two new files hold it. The Dockerfile, in the explorer, starts from a slim Python image, installs boto three, copies the app in and runs it as an unprivileged user. The file in the editor is the task definition, which tells E C S how to run that image. It is for Fargate, so there are no servers to manage. Lines five and six ask for five hundred and twelve C P U units, half a virtual C P U, and one gibibyte of memory, and line seven asks for the Arm architecture, Graviton again. Lines nine and ten name two roles, which is the part people most often confuse. The execution role, OrderApiExecution, is what E C S itself uses to pull the image from E C R and to write the container's logs. The task role, OrderApi, the same role as before, is what the app's own code may call. The container's image is in the shop's E C R repository, tag one point four point two, and line sixteen sets a stop timeout of thirty seconds: when E C S stops a task it sends SIGTERM, waits thirty seconds, and only then kills it. In the terminal, an E C R repository is created and its U R I printed, and the task definition is registered: family order api, revision one, five hundred and twelve, one thousand and twenty four. The table compares a server and a task. The unit is a server or a task. A server is built from an image and user data; a task from a container image. Operating system patches are the shop's on E C two and A W S's on Fargate. Next, whether the shop should run Kubernetes instead.

Kubernetes is the other common way to run containers, and on A W S it is E K S. On the left is what the order A P I would look like as a Kubernetes deployment. It is illustrative, not run. It asks for three replicas of a container named app, from the same image in E C R, on port eight zero eight zero. It is not much longer than the task definition, and that is not where the cost is. The table is the honest trade. Kubernetes buys one A P I that works the same across clouds and data centres; it costs a cluster that has to be upgraded several times a year, because each Kubernetes version is supported for a limited time. It buys a large ecosystem, Helm charts and operators for almost anything; it costs add-ons, node groups and networking plugins that someone must choose, configure and keep current. It buys fine control over scheduling; it costs a second permission system, Kubernetes R B A C, beside I A M. And it buys a platform that many teams can share; it costs people who know it well. E K S runs the control plane for you, for a fee per cluster hour, but everything else on that list stays with you. The list is the verdict for the shop. One service, one team, one cloud: Kubernetes is not the requirement. E C S on Fargate runs the same image with no cluster to upgrade and no second permission system. Choose E K S when the requirement is Kubernetes itself: many teams sharing a platform, portability across environments, or an ecosystem the business depends on. Picking it because it is popular means paying its costs without collecting its benefits. Next, the property every one of these options assumes: servers that can disappear without losing anything.

Auto Scaling removes servers as well as adding them, so a server must hold nothing that matters. The terminal starts with a model, carts dot p y. Three hundred shoppers fill carts behind a round robin load balancer, so each of three servers creates one hundred. Then a scale-in terminates app two, and its disk with it. With carts on each server's own disk, two hundred are kept and one hundred are lost, a hundred shoppers whose carts vanish mid-purchase. With carts in a shared store, all three hundred are kept and none are lost. The table on the right is the rule that follows: product data lives in S three, carts in a shared store and orders in the database, both from Course nine, and the server's own disk holds nothing that matters. The second half is about how a server leaves. The editor shows the end of app server dot p y, now with a stop function on line thirty six. When the process receives SIGTERM, the signal E C S, Auto Scaling and systemd all send before stopping something, it prints that it accepts no new requests and finishes those in flight, and line thirty eight shuts the server down from another thread. Line forty three installs the handler. Line forty six, after the server loop ends, waits for request threads to finish before exiting. In the terminal, the real app starts, answers a health check, and is sent SIGTERM; its log shows the request, the message, and stopped cleanly. The list puts the sequence together. The load balancer stops sending new requests first, through deregistration. SIGTERM tells the app to finish what is in flight. It exits before the timeout kills it. And since any server may be the one that goes, none may hold a cart. That completes the compute course. Next course, making all of this repeatable.

Six courses of scripts have built the shop, and this one starts by running one of them again. The account already has the network and its security groups. In the terminal, infra zero five network runs a second time, and nothing stops it: create V P C does not ask whether a V P C called shop prod already exists, so the script makes a second one, with nine more subnets, and prints them all. Describing the V P Cs named shop prod now finds two, with the same range, and nothing but their I Ds to tell them apart. Then the filters script runs again. It looks up the V P C by name and takes the first of the two, which is the original, and tries to create s g a l b in it. That group already exists, and the call fails: invalid group dot duplicate. The table sums up what happened. The network script made a duplicate, because a create call never asks what exists. The lookup found two, because a name tag is a label, not an identity. And the filters script failed half way, because it picked a V P C that was already full. Now imagine this in production at night, with someone trying to fix one subnet. The list names the underlying problem. A script records steps to take, not the result you want. Run twice, it does the steps twice, or fails part of the way through and leaves things half built. And nothing records which resources the script made, so nothing can safely change or remove them later, short of a teardown script that has to be kept exactly in step. Every script in infra has this property. The rest of this course replaces them, starting with the network, with templates that describe the result instead. Next, what declaring infrastructure actually means.

On the left is the same network written two ways. The script, in red at the top, is a list of steps: create a V P C, keep its I D in a variable, create subnet public a in it, then public b, and so on. The template, in green below it, describes the result: there is a V P C with this range, and a subnet called public a whose V P C is that V P C, with this range. It never says create. A service, CloudFormation, compares the template with what already exists and works out the calls itself. The table compares them. The script says what to do; the template says what should exist. Run the script twice and it does everything twice; deploy the template twice and the second time there is nothing to change. The script does not know what it made; the template's stack records every resource it created. The script runs in the order it is written; the template's order comes from its references, so a subnet that names the V P C is created after it. And removing everything means a separate teardown script for the one, and deleting the stack for the other. The list below the table is what a stack holds. Desired state: the template itself, which can be reviewed and versioned like the app's code. Ownership: the stack knows exactly which physical resources belong to it, so it can change and delete them safely. Dependencies: references like Ref and GetAtt decide the order, and the parallelism. And repeatability: the same template builds the same thing in any account, at any time, which is what Course thirteen's second Region would need. Declaring infrastructure does not remove the need to understand the A P I calls; the earlier courses were not wasted. It moves the work of getting from what exists to what should exist onto a service. Next, the shop's first stack.

The file in the editor is templates slash network dot yaml, the network from Course five, declared. It describes a resource called V P C, of type A W S E C two V P C, with the range ten dot twenty slash sixteen and the name shop prod. Then nine subnets, of which two are visible. Each names its V P C with Ref V P C, which is both a value and a dependency: CloudFormation creates the V P C first and passes its I D. And each picks its zone with Select over Get A Zs, the list of the Region's zones, rather than naming eu west two a, so the template works unchanged in another Region. In the terminal, in a fresh account, cfn lint checks the template first, against A W S's resource specifications, and finds nothing. An earlier draft that named the zones directly drew a warning for each one, which is why it changed. Then aws cloudformation deploy creates a stack called shop network: it makes a change set, executes it, and reports success. The same deploy, run again, makes a change set, finds it empty, and says there are no changes to deploy: the stack is up to date. Compare that with the last two sections. Describing the stack's resources counts ten: the V P C and nine subnets, all owned by the stack. The table on the right is that difference. The first deploy created ten resources. The second did nothing. After an edit, a deploy changes only the difference. The list adds the rest. cfn lint checks a template before A W S sees it. Ref orders the work. Get A Zs keeps zones out of the template. And deleting the stack removes all ten resources, in the right order, with nothing left behind. Next, parameters, outputs, and how one stack uses another's resources.

The shop is not one big template; each concern is its own stack, and stacks need to refer to each other. The file in the editor is templates slash filters dot yaml, the security group chain from Course five, declared. It starts with a parameter, AppPort, a number with a default of eight zero eight zero: a value supplied when the stack is deployed. The app group's V P C is Import Value shop V P C I D, a value the network stack offered. Its rule admits the AppPort parameter, through Ref, and only from the load balancer's group, through GetAtt AlbGroup dot GroupId, an attribute of another resource in this template. And at the bottom, an output that exports the app group's I D as shop s g app, offering it to any later stack.
