In the terminal, the filters stack is created with AppPort eight zero eight zero, the waiter returns when creation is complete, and describing the stack shows create complete and the parameter's value. Listing exports shows the whole contract between stacks: the network stack's V P C, app subnets and data subnets, and the filters stack's two groups. Course nine's database template will import the data subnets and the database group. The table names the four ways a template refers: Ref for a parameter or a resource's I D, GetAtt for an attribute, Export to offer a value, and Import Value to use one from another stack. CloudFormation also protects the contract: an export cannot be changed or removed while another stack imports it. The list is the one thing never to do with any of this. A secret, like a database password, never goes in a template or a parameter default, because anyone who can read the stack can read it. Use a dynamic reference to Secrets Manager, or let the service manage the secret, as the database does in Course nine. Next, previewing a change before it happens.

A change to a template is a change to production, so CloudFormation can show you a change set first: every resource the update would add, modify or remove, and whether it would be replaced. Replacement is the word that matters, because replacing a V P C means a new V P C. The emulator's change sets do not carry that detail, so this section reads it where CloudFormation does: from each resource type's schema, which lists its create only properties, the ones that cannot change in place. The tool in the editor, replacement preview, does exactly that, using the schemas A W S publishes, which ship with cfn lint. Line twenty one reads the old and new templates. For each resource it finds the changed properties, and on line twenty seven, any property that refers to a resource already being replaced. Line twenty nine keeps those that are create only. If any remain, the resource is replaced. In the terminal, someone widens the V P C from slash sixteen to slash fifteen, a one-character edit, and the preview runs on the old and new templates. The V P C is replaced, because CidrBlock is create only. Then all nine subnets are replaced too, because each names the V P C in VpcId, which is also create only. Ten of ten resources replaced, from one character. The list names the safe alternative: add a secondary range to the existing V P C, which is a separate resource and replaces nothing. The table is what a change set can and cannot tell you. It tells you which resources change, which are replaced, and in what order. It cannot tell you whether a call will fail, what happens to the data in a replaced resource, or what the app does in the meantime. And drift detection answers the reverse question: what changed outside the stack, by hand, since it was deployed. Next, when an update fails part way through.

When an update fails part way, CloudFormation rolls the stack back to the previous template. That protects the infrastructure. It does not protect the data, and the file in the editor is about the data: templates slash orders d b dot yaml, the orders database that Course nine creates. Lines thirteen and fourteen are the protection. Deletion policy snapshot means that if the stack is deleted, a final snapshot of the database is kept. Update replace policy snapshot means the same if an update replaces it, which the last section showed can happen from one line. Line twenty two encrypts the storage. Line twenty four turns on deletion protection, so the database cannot be deleted at all until someone turns it off on purpose. Line twenty six lets R D S create and keep the master password in Secrets Manager, so no password appears anywhere in this file. In the terminal, cfn lint finds nothing in the template. Then a copy is made without the update replace policy, and cfn lint warns: both update replace policy and deletion policy are needed to protect the resource. With only one of them, an update that replaces the database would delete the old one. The table on the right is an illustrative failed update, not a captured one. At eighteen thirty nine, version fifteen's migration adds a column to the orders table. At eighteen forty one, a resource in version fifteen fails. The stack rolls back, and by eighteen forty four version fourteen is restored. But the list names what rollback cannot undo: the migration ran, and the column stays. A rollback restores the template, not the state of the data. So the rule is to make every change one the previous version can live with, like adding a column before using it, and to protect stateful resources on both delete and replace. Next, releasing the app itself, safely.

Infrastructure changes rarely; the app changes all the time, and the stacks and the pipeline now light up on the map. Order A P I one point five point zero has a bug: two percent of its requests fail. How much damage that does depends on how it is released. The table gives the three ways. All at once, or rolling, replaces the old version on the servers in batches, and rolling back means deploying the old version again. Blue green with a linear shift starts a second set of servers and moves ten percent more of the traffic to it each minute; rolling back means shifting the traffic back. Blue green with a canary sends ten percent first, waits, then sends the rest. The terminal is a model, run locally, not a measurement. It assumes the evening peak of five hundred and sixty requests a second, and an error alarm that stops the release after two minutes. All at once, every request goes to the new version for those two minutes: one thousand three hundred and forty four failed requests before the alarm. Linear, ten then twenty percent of the traffic: two hundred and two. Canary, ten percent for both minutes: one hundred and thirty four. The same bug costs a tenth as much, because less traffic was exposed while the alarm made up its mind. The list is how the shop releases. Build once: one image with one digest, tested, and never rebuilt for production. Deploy with an identity of its own, never a person's credentials. Let CodeDeploy shift the load balancer's traffic, with a configuration such as E C S linear ten percent every one minute. And attach the error alarm, so the shift stops and reverses by itself. Next, how one artefact moves from the development account to production.

The last piece is how a release crosses from the development account into production without anyone carrying credentials across. The first table follows commit nine f three c two e one. It is built once, in the dev account, into one image whose digest is recorded. That same digest is deployed to dev and tested. Then the pipeline deploys the same digest to production, by assuming a role there called ShopDeploy. What reaches production is byte for byte what was tested, never a rebuild. The policy in the middle is ShopDeploy's trust policy, and it is the gate. Its one statement, only the shop pipeline, allows s t s assume role, and its principal is a single role, ShopPipeline, in the dev account, four four four four, five five five five, six six six six. Its condition requires the caller to belong to the shop's organization. So no person can assume ShopDeploy, and no other role can either, not even another role in dev. ShopDeploy's own permissions, not shown, cover deploying the shop's stacks and services and nothing else. Production changes happen through this one door, which is also the door CloudTrail watches in Course twelve. The last table compares the tools for writing the templates themselves. CloudFormation is YAML or JSON, and its state is kept by the stack, in A W S. The C D K is code, in TypeScript or Python, that generates CloudFormation, so its state is also a stack. Terraform is its own language, works across providers, and keeps state in a file you must store and lock yourself. All three end in the same A P I calls; the choice is about the team, not A W S. That completes the infrastructure: declared, reviewed, promoted. Next course, where the shop's files live.

Storage on A W S comes in three shapes, and choosing well starts with how the bytes are read and written. On the left is object storage, S three. You store and fetch whole objects by key, over H T T P S, and you cannot edit part of one in place: you replace it. Any number of readers can fetch it, from anywhere, and the data is Regional, kept in three or more zones. The shop uses it for products, photos and reports. In the middle is block storage, E B S. It is a disk: any byte can be read or written, as with a local drive, but it is attached to one instance, in one zone. It survives a reboot, and a snapshot of it survives the loss of that zone. The shop uses it for each server's own disk, and for a volume the invoice service writes to. On the right is file storage, E F S. It is a shared folder, mounted over N F S by many servers at once, in every zone, and it grows and shrinks with what is stored. The shop uses it for invoices that several app servers write. The table matches needs to kinds. Files served to browsers, at any scale: S three. A database's or an operating system's own disk: E B S. One folder written by many servers: E F S. And for Windows file shares, high performance computing, NetApp or Z F S, the matching kind of F S x. The list is what each survives, which is what Course six's stateless servers rely on. When a server is replaced, S three and E F S are untouched, while its E B S disk is deleted by default. When a zone is lost, S three and E F S keep serving, while that zone's E B S volumes go with it. And a mistaken delete is undone only by versioning or a backup, the subject of the last sections. Next, the catalog bucket, declared.

The buckets the scripts made in Course three are now declared, in templates slash storage dot yaml, shown on the right. The catalog bucket is named after the account, as before, and blocks all public access, so no policy or A C L can make it public by accident. The part shown is its bucket policy with one statement, H T T P S only: it denies every action, by anyone, on the bucket and everything in it, whenever the request did not arrive over T L S. That deny cannot be overridden by any allow. In the terminal, the storage stack is created, and the waiter returns when it is complete. Then the first product is put: its key is products slash p dash one thousand and one dot json, its content type J S O N, and S three returns its E tag. Getting it back returns the same length, one thousand eight hundred and thirty four bytes, the same type and the same E tag. Listing everything under the prefix products slash finds that one key. The list on the right is how S three names things, because it is easy to picture it as a file system and be surprised. A key is a flat name. The slash in products slash p dash one thousand and one is just a character; there is no products folder, only a prefix that listings and the console group by. A put replaces a whole object, so there is no appending to one or changing part of it. And every bucket the shop owns blocks public access, while the catalog's policy also refuses plain H T T P. This is the bucket the order A P I from Course six reads every product page from. Next, letting shoppers upload photos to S three without ever holding an A W S key.

Shoppers can attach a photo to a review. The photo should go straight to S three, not through the app servers, and a shopper's browser must never hold an A W S key. A presigned U R L does both. In the editor, lines eleven to thirteen are the app's side: boto three signs, but does not send, a put object request for one key in the uploads bucket, reviews slash p dash one thousand and one slash photo seventy seven dot j p g, with content type j p e g, valid for three hundred seconds. The signing is the same signature version four from Course two, carried in the U R L's query string instead of a header. The next lines take the U R L apart. In the terminal: the endpoint is S three in E U west two; the path is the bucket and the key; it expires in three hundred seconds; and it was signed by the app's access key. Lines twenty one to twenty three are the browser's side: a plain H T T P put of the photo's bytes to that U R L, with the same content type, and no credentials at all. S three answers two hundred, and the object is stored. The table is the whole flow in four steps: the browser asks the app for an upload U R L, the app signs one, the browser puts to S three directly, and S three checks the signature before accepting it. The list is what the U R L carries, and therefore what it risks. It allows one method, on one key, with one content type. It borrows the signer's permission, so the app's role must be allowed to put that object. It expires, here after five minutes, and never later than the credentials that signed it. And it contains a signature, not the key itself. Anyone who gets the U R L in that time can use it, so keep the expiry short. Next, two jobs writing the same object at once.

Two background jobs update the same product file. One lowers the price from twelve pounds to ten; the other decrements the stock when an item sells. The code in the editor stages that race. Line twenty four has both jobs read the file first, before either writes, which is exactly what happens when they run at the same moment. The price job writes its change on line twenty six. The stock job writes on line twenty nine, based on what it read, which no longer reflects the price change. In the terminal, the plain race ends with price twelve and stock thirty nine: the price change is lost, silently, because the last writer won. The table on the right is that sequence. S three is not wrong here: it is strongly consistent, so any read after a write sees that write, but two separate requests are not a transaction, and nothing stopped the second write from overwriting the first. The fix is a conditional write. Each job remembers the E tag it read, and writes with If Match that E tag: only if the object is still the one it read. Run again with conditions, the price job writes first and succeeds. The stock job's write is refused, with precondition failed, because the E tag has changed. It re-reads, applies its change to the new version, and writes again. The run ends with price ten and stock thirty nine, both changes kept. The list sums it up. A read after a write sees that write. Two writes to one key: the last one wins. If Match makes a write conditional on nothing having changed. And when several objects must change together, all or nothing, the right tool is a database with transactions, which is Course nine. Next, keeping every version of an object, and choosing how long to keep them.

Versioning changes what a write and a delete mean. In the terminal, versioning is turned on for the catalog bucket, and a lifecycle configuration is applied from a new file, catalog lifecycle dot json. Then versions dot p y runs. In the editor, lines sixteen and seventeen put the product twice, at twelve pounds and then ten, and each put creates a version with its own I D. Line eighteen deletes the product. With versioning on, a delete does not remove anything; it adds a delete marker on top, and the terminal confirms the delete made a marker. Reading the key now returns no such key, because the marker is the current version. But reading version one by its I D still returns twelve pounds: nothing was lost. Line twenty two removes the delete marker itself, by its version I D, and reading the key again returns the latest real version, ten pounds. The product is restored. One emulator note: its listing of versions mislabels which one is latest after a delete, so the script follows the version I Ds each call returns instead. The table on the right is the lifecycle file. Old versions expire thirty days after they stop being current, so versioning does not grow the bill forever. Objects under exports slash move to standard infrequent access after thirty days, and to Glacier after ninety. The list is the catch. Infrequent access is cheaper to keep but charges for every gigabyte read, with a thirty day minimum. Glacier is cheaper still, but a restore takes minutes to hours. Old versions cost the same as any other data while they exist. And versioning undoes a delete in this bucket; it is not a backup, because whoever can delete the bucket can delete its versions too. Next, disks and shared folders.

The invoice service keeps its working files on an E B S volume, and it needs to move from zone a to zone b. In the terminal, the first command creates a thirty gibibyte g p three volume in E U west two a and prints its I D. A volume is zonal: it can only be attached to an instance in that zone. The second command takes a snapshot of it. A snapshot is stored by A W S at the Region's level, out of sight, in S three, so it is no longer tied to zone a. The waiter returns when the snapshot is complete. The fourth command creates a new volume from the snapshot, in E U west two b, and it comes back thirty gibibytes, in zone b. That is the only way to move a disk between zones, and also how a disk survives the loss of its zone: by having been snapshotted before. The table on the right sums up the move: the volume lives in zone a only, its snapshot lives in the Region, and the new volume lives in zone b. The last command creates an E F S file system for the invoices, shop invoices one, encrypted, and it is available. An E F S file system is Regional, and each zone gets a mount target, so servers in all three zones mount the same folder at slash m n t slash invoices and see the same files. That makes it the shared-folder answer that E B S cannot be. The second table is the wider choice for shared files. Linux servers sharing a folder: E F S. Windows file shares: F S x for Windows File Server. Fast scratch space for big compute jobs: F S x for Lustre. NetApp or Z F S features: F S x for NetApp ONTAP or OpenZFS. Next, encrypting data, and what each kind of protection actually protects against.

The sales reports are the shop's most sensitive files, and the editor shows the part of the storage template that protects them: a K M S key and its alias. Line thirty one makes it a K M S key, and line thirty four turns on automatic rotation, so the key material changes every year without anyone re-encrypting anything. Lines thirty eight to forty one are its key policy, the resource policy of a key: it lets the account administer the key, and any use of the key must also be allowed by I A M. Course twelve adds the auditor's permission to decrypt. On the map, K M S keys now light up. In the terminal, the reports bucket gets default encryption from a new file, using the shop reports key, with a bucket key enabled. A bucket key means S three asks K M S for a short-lived key for the bucket, rather than calling K M S for every object, which cuts K M S requests and their cost. Reading the setting back shows the bucket key is on, and putting a report shows it was encrypted with K M S, with the bucket key. The table on the right is the point of this section, because each protection answers a different threat. A stolen disk: encryption at rest. The wrong reader: the key policy and the bucket policy, since reading requires permission to decrypt. A mistaken delete: versioning. A lost Region: replication to another Region. A deleted or compromised account: a backup kept elsewhere, in another account, which is Course twelve's job. And deliberate wiping by someone with permission: Object Lock, which makes versions undeletable for a set time. Encryption alone protects against none of the last four. That completes the shop's files. Next course, its orders, in databases.

Before the shop picks a database, it writes down what it will ask of its data, because the engine follows from the questions, not the other way round. The table at the top is the shop's evening peak, and the rates are assumptions. Showing a product page is about four hundred and fifty reads a second, always by product id, and it must be fast, though a price a minute old is acceptable. Placing an order is only about six writes a second, but it must be all or nothing, and it must never sell stock the shop does not have. A customer's own order list is about forty reads a second, by customer, newest first, and it must be up to date. Sales by day is a few queries a day that scan everything in a date range, and that belongs to Course eleven. The middle row is three ways to model data. Relational, in R D S, keeps rows in tables linked by keys, changes many rows in one transaction, and answers any question you can write in S Q L: the shop's orders, order lines and stock. Key value, in Dynamo D B, reads and writes each item by its key, with steady latency however large the table grows, but it only answers the questions its keys were designed for: a customer's orders. In memory, in ElastiCache, is a copy held close to the app, answered in microseconds, which expires or is deleted when the data changes, and is never the only copy: the product pages. The list at the bottom is five questions to answer before choosing an engine. Which keys does every read and write name? What must change together, or not at all? How stale may a read be: never, or a minute? How fast does the data grow, and how long is it kept? And who runs it: patching, backups and failover? Next, the orders database itself, as a managed R D S instance.

The map now shows the orders database, inside the V P C. It was declared in Course seven, in templates slash orders dash d b dot yaml, and this section creates it. The excerpt on the right is the instance. The engine is PostgreSQL, version sixteen point nine, on a d b dot r seven g dot large, a Graviton class with plenty of memory for a database. Storage is encrypted, and Multi A Z is true, which keeps a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone. Deletion protection is on. The master password is never written anywhere: manage master user password tells R D S to create it and keep it in Secrets Manager. The instance sits in the subnet group of the three data subnets, and behind the security group s g dash d b, which only accepts port five four three two from the app servers. In the terminal, the stack is created against the emulator, and the waiter returns when it is complete. Describing the instance reads back postgres, sixteen point nine, the class, Multi A Z true and encrypted true. The subnet group is shop dash data, with seven days of automated backups. And the endpoint is a D N S name in E U west two: the app connects to that name, never to an address, because a failover moves the name to the standby. The emulator records what the template asked for, but it does not run PostgreSQL behind it, so the next section runs the same engine locally. The table at the bottom is what managed covers. R D S patches the hardware, the operating system and the engine; the shop still owns its schema, its indexes and its queries. R D S takes backups and offers point in time restore; the shop still has to test that a restore works. R D S keeps a standby and fails over; the app still has to reconnect. And R D S keeps the master password in Secrets Manager; the shop still decides who may read that secret. Aurora is a different engine family, compatible with PostgreSQL, whose storage spans three zones; it comes back in section five. Next, placing an order inside a transaction.

Order five hundred and one is two of product p one thousand and one at ten pounds, and two of p one thousand and two at four pounds fifty, twenty nine pounds in all. But only one p one thousand and two is left. Next, how the app servers connect to this database, and where the password comes from.

Every app server needs two things before it can place an order: the database's password, and a connection. The editor shows tools slash connections dot py. Its first part reads the credentials. In A W S, R D S creates that secret itself, named R D S, exclamation mark, d b, dash and the instance's resource id, and rotates it. The emulator does not create it, so this step's setup stores a secret of the same shape. In the terminal, listing secrets finds it: its A R N, in E U west two, ends with that name and a random suffix. Running the script reads user shop and a thirty two character password, without the password ever being in a file. The second part is the connection budget. PostgreSQL limits how many connections it accepts. Two hundred is assumed here, because the real figure depends on the instance's memory and its parameter group, so check that. Ten are reserved for administrators and replication, which leaves one hundred and ninety. Each app server opens a pool of twenty. Three servers want sixty, six want one hundred and twenty, nine want one hundred and eighty, all fine. But on a busy evening, Auto Scaling grows the group to twelve servers, which want two hundred and forty, and fifty connections are refused. Scaling out the app made checkout fail. The table on the right is where the password is not. Not in the code or a template, because it stays in git forever. Not in the server image, because every copy carries it. Not in an environment file, because it never rotates. In Secrets Manager, read at start up: yes. The list is what to do when servers outgrow connections. Use smaller pools: fifteen each fits twelve servers. Use R D S Proxy, which keeps one shared pool for every client. Choose a larger instance with more memory. And alarm on the connection count, before the errors start. Next, keeping the database available, and getting it back when something goes wrong.

R D S offers five things that sound alike, and the table at the top says what each one is for. A Multi A Z D B instance, the shop's choice, keeps one standby in another zone, written synchronously. It cannot be read, and it exists only to take over: failover typically takes one to two minutes. A Multi A Z D B cluster has a writer and two standbys in three zones, the standbys can serve reads, and failover is typically under thirty five seconds. Aurora is a separate engine family whose storage volume itself spans three zones; it can have up to fifteen replicas, and failover is typically about thirty seconds. A read replica is an asynchronous copy, in any zone or even another Region: it takes reading load away from the primary, but it is not a backup, because it can lag behind. And point in time restore creates a brand new instance from the automated backups and transaction logs, at any second within the retention period, which is seven days for the shop. The row below takes three bad evenings. First, E U west two b goes dark. With Multi A Z, the standby takes over, and the endpoint's name stays the same, so the app reconnects to the same name; transactions that were open at that moment are lost and must be retried. Second, order history is slow, because reports are scanning the primary. A read replica takes the history queries, but it lags, so a customer should never read their own fresh order from it; writes still all go to the one primary. Third, and the case people get wrong: a migration drops a column. The standby dropped it too, within milliseconds, because that is what synchronous means. Multi A Z protects against losing a zone, not against a mistake. Point in time restore to eighteen thirty nine, one minute before the migration, creates a new instance, and the missing data is copied back from it. Next, a different kind of database: a key value table in Dynamo D B.

The customer's order list is a good fit for a key value table: every read names one customer, and wants their orders newest first. The table on the right is the design. The Orders table's partition key is customer, so all of c seventeen's orders live together. Its sort key, s k, is the order's time, a hash mark and its id, so a customer's orders are stored in time order. An index named by status lets the shop ask for every placed order. The table is on demand, billed per request, with no capacity to plan. The editor shows tools slash orders table dot py, which creates the table and puts six orders into the emulator. Line twenty nine queries c seventeen's partition, with scan index forward false, so newest first. The terminal prints o five fourteen, o five eleven, then o five oh one. Line thirty four queries the same partition with a range on the sort key, between the eleventh and the thirteenth of October, and gets the two orders from the twelfth. Line thirty nine queries the index for placed, and gets four orders from three customers. The last line counts the index's key values, and this is the problem: status only ever has two values, placed and shipped. Dynamo D B spreads a table across partitions by the partition key, so every write to the index lands on one of only two keys. At the shop's evening peak, all new orders would hit the same one, a hot key, throttled while the rest of the table sits idle. The list on the right says the rule. The keys are the questions: a query names one partition key, and the sort key gives order and ranges. A key with two values is a hot key. A better index key is status plus the day, which spreads the writes, and asks for one day's placed orders at a time. Notice what Dynamo D B does not offer here: a join, or a question its keys do not answer. Next, selling the last unit in stock, safely.

There is one p one thousand and two left, and two orders arrive for it. In a key value table, the safety comes from conditions, and from a transaction across two tables. The editor shows tools slash last unit dot py. Its place function writes two things at once, with transact write items on line seventeen. The first action takes the stock: set stock to stock minus the quantity, but only on condition, on line twenty one, that stock is at least that quantity. The second action records the order in the Orders table, on condition, on line twenty six, that no order with that id exists yet, so a retried request cannot place it twice. Dynamo D B applies both actions, or neither. If any condition fails, line twenty nine catches the cancelled transaction, and line thirty prints the reason for each action. In the terminal, run against the emulator, o six oh one is placed. O six oh two is cancelled, with the reasons conditional check failed for the stock, and none for the order, so the table says exactly which check refused it. Afterwards stock is zero and there is one order. Nothing was oversold, and the code never had to read the stock, compare it and hope nothing changed in between: the table refuses, not the code. The table on the right is the other half: which read sees the last write. A default read is eventually consistent, and usually sees a write within a second. A read with consistent read set to true always sees it, at twice the read cost. A query on a global secondary index is always eventually consistent. And inside a transaction, a write sees what it committed. The final stock line in the script uses a consistent read. The list sums it up. The condition stock at least the quantity is checked at the moment of the write. Both actions happen, or neither. O six oh two is told why. And retrying it can never oversell. Next, putting a cache in front of the product page, and the stale price that comes with it.

Four hundred and fifty product page reads a second do not need four hundred and fifty database queries a second, because the product barely changes. A cache keeps a copy close to the app, and the usual pattern is cache aside. The editor shows tools slash cache aside dot py, a model of the pattern in plain Python, with no A W S service involved, so the terminal is not marked emulated. On a read, line twelve looks in the cache, and if the entry is there and not expired, line thirteen returns it, labelled stale if it no longer matches the database. On a miss, line fourteen loads the price from the database and keeps a copy that expires after the T T L, sixty seconds. On a write, line nineteen updates the database, and if invalidation is on, line twenty deletes the cached copy, so the next read loads the new one. The script reads at zero, the price drops from twelve to ten at ten seconds, and it reads again at twenty, forty and sixty one. The terminal shows both strategies. With the T T L only, the read at zero misses and loads twelve. At twenty and forty, shoppers are shown twelve, stale, because the cache still holds the old copy. Only at sixty one, after the copy expires, does a miss load ten. With delete on write, the price change deletes the copy, so the read at twenty misses and loads ten, and later reads are hits on the fresh price. The table on the right is the summary: T T L only is stale from ten seconds to sixty; delete on write is not stale here; and no cache is never stale, but every read goes to the database. The list gives the rules. The T T L is the worst case staleness, so choose it on purpose. Delete on write, but keep the T T L too, in case a delete is lost. Never cache the stock count that an order depends on. And the managed cache on A W S is ElastiCache, for example with Valkey. Next, moving an existing database into R D S, and the engines the shop does not need.

Suppose the shop's orders still lived in an old data centre's PostgreSQL. A W S Database Migration Service, D M S, moves them into R D S without stopping the shop. The editor shows infra slash oh nine migration dot s h. Two small functions come first. One reads a password from Secrets Manager, and one creates a D M S endpoint: a description of a database, its engine, host, port and credentials. Line twelve creates the source endpoint, the data centre's database, and line thirteen the target, the R D S instance. Lines fifteen to eighteen create a replication instance, the server that does the copying. The replication task joins them. Its migration type, on line twenty two, is full load and C D C: copy every existing row once, then keep applying every change the source records, change data capture, until the shop is ready to cut over. The table mappings file selects every table in the schema shop. In the terminal, against the emulator, the R D S host is exported, the script creates the task, orders to R D S, full load and C D C, creating, and starting it reports running. The emulator only records the task; it moves no data. The table is the engines the shop does not need, each built for a different question. Document D B stores J S O N documents. Neptune stores graphs of relations, such as who bought what with whom. Timestream stores time series. Open Search answers full text search. And Keyspaces runs Cassandra. Each one is right for its question; the shop's questions are a relational order, a key value list and a cached page, so it stays with R D S, Dynamo D B and a cache. That completes the shop's data: orders in PostgreSQL, a customer's history in Dynamo D B, and product pages in a cache. Next, in Course ten, the checkout itself is taken apart into an A P I, functions, queues and events.

Until now, the order A P I ran on the shop's own servers behind the load balancer. This course takes the checkout apart, starting with a managed front door: A P I Gateway, now lit on the map. The script on the right, infra slash ten dash A P I dot s h, builds a rest A P I named shop dash A P I with one resource, slash orders. Before it, the script creates a Cognito user pool called shoppers, where shoppers' accounts live. Three things are attached to the post method. A request validator named body only checks every request body against the Order model, a J S O N schema in infra slash A P I: a customer id, and at least one line, each with a product and a quantity of one or more.
