Its integration is a mock for now, until the function in the next section exists. Finally the A P I is deployed to a stage named prod, throttled to six hundred requests a second with bursts of up to twelve hundred. In the terminal, against the emulator, the script prints the A P I's id. Reading the method back shows Cognito user pools as its authorization, a validator attached, and the Order model. The stage reads back six hundred and twelve hundred. The table at the bottom is the point of all this: requests that are turned away before any of the shop's code runs. No token, or a bad one, gets four oh one from the authorizer. A body with no lines, or a quantity of zero, gets four hundred from the validator. Above six hundred a second, the stage answers four two nine, too many requests. Only a request that passes all three reaches the integration. The emulator records this configuration but does not enforce it; those answers are A P I Gateway's documented behaviour. Next, the function that places the order.

The order is now placed by a Lambda function, place dash order, whose code is in functions slash place order slash handler dot p y. The editor shows its two parts. Lines seven to ten are initialisation. They run once, when Lambda starts a new execution environment for the function, which is called a cold start: they create the Dynamo D B client and read the two table names from the environment. The counter on line ten lives in that environment too. Then line thirteen is the handler, which Lambda calls for every request. It counts the call, reads the order from the request body, and on line nineteen runs the same transaction as Course nine: take the stock on condition that enough is left, and record the order on condition that it is new. A success returns two oh one, created; a cancelled transaction returns four oh nine, conflict. In the terminal, infra slash ten dash function dot s h zips the handler and creates the function in the emulator: place dash order, Python three point thirteen, on arm sixty four, with five hundred and twelve megabytes and a ten second timeout. The emulator can create a function but cannot run its code, so tools slash invoke local dot p y does what the Lambda runtime does: it imports the handler module once, which runs the initialisation, and then calls the handler for two orders against the emulator's tables. O six oh one gets two oh one, call one. O six oh two, for the same last unit, gets four oh nine, and it is call two: the same environment, reused, so the client was not created again. The table on the right is the function's configuration. Memory also sets its share of C P U. The timeout stops an invocation after ten seconds. The environment holds table names, never secrets. Its role, place order F N, comes next. And the list is the life cycle: initialise once, then call after call, and globals survive between calls, so never rely on them being fresh or shared. Next, how many copies of this function can run at once.

A function runs with the permissions of its execution role, and as many copies at once as there are requests in flight. Both need limits. The editor shows policies slash place order F N dot j s o n, the role's permissions. It allows exactly two actions, update item and put item, on exactly two tables, Stock and Orders, in this account and Region: what the transaction needs and nothing else. In the terminal, the policy is put on the role place order F N, and the A W S managed policy for basic Lambda execution is attached, which lets the function write its own logs to CloudWatch. Then the function gets a reserved concurrency of fifty. The emulator echoes fifty back. Tools slash concurrency dot p y does the arithmetic, shown again in the table on the right. At the evening peak there are five hundred and sixty requests a second, and each invocation is assumed to take a hundred and twenty milliseconds. Requests in flight are the rate times the duration, which is Little's law: sixty seven at once. With fifty reserved, the function can finish at most four hundred and seventeen a second, so a hundred and forty three requests a second are throttled, and A P I Gateway answers them with four two nine. That sounds like a mistake, so why cap it? The list gives the reasons. Reserved concurrency is a ceiling for whatever is behind the function: never more than fifty writers at once. If it wrote to the orders database instead of Dynamo D B, every environment would hold its own connection, and Course nine showed what happens when connections run out. It is also a guarantee: fifty of the account's concurrency, a thousand per Region by default, are always kept for place order, whatever other functions do. If fifty is too low for the peak, either raise it, measured against what is behind it, or stop making the shopper wait, by putting the work on a queue. And the role grants the two tables plus its logs. Next, that queue.

Shipping an order does not need to happen while the shopper waits. The order is placed, a message goes onto a queue, and a fulfilment worker takes it from there, at its own pace. The editor shows tools slash consumer dot p y, run against the emulator. Earlier in the file, it creates a standard S Q S queue named fulfilment, with a visibility timeout of thirty seconds, and sends three orders: five oh one, five oh two and five oh three. Line eighteen receives them with long polling, which waits up to twenty seconds for messages instead of returning empty at once. For each message the worker does its work and then, on line twenty three, deletes it. But for o five oh three, line twenty one simulates a crash: the worker dies after receiving the message and before deleting it. In the terminal, five oh one and five oh two are shipped and deleted. Five oh three is received and the worker crashes. Line twenty six receives again, immediately, and gets nothing: o five oh three is still in the queue, but invisible, because receiving a message hides it for the visibility timeout rather than removing it. The replay does not wait thirty seconds; line twenty eight ends the timeout by hand. The next receive gets o five oh three back, with a receive count of two, and this time it is shipped and deleted. Nothing was lost, although a worker died holding it. The list on the right is the rule. Received is hidden, not removed. If it is not deleted, it comes back. So the visibility timeout must be longer than the work takes, or a slow worker's message is handed to a second worker while the first is still on it. And the checkout no longer waits for any of this. The table compares the two queue types. Standard delivers at least once, in roughly the order sent, with nearly unlimited throughput. F I F O delivers exactly once and in order within a group, with limited throughput. Fulfilment does not need strict order, so it is standard. Next, telling several services about the same order.

When an order is placed, fulfilment is not the only service that cares. Loyalty points must be added, and large orders must be checked for fraud. Rather than the order code sending three messages, it publishes one, to an S N S topic, and the topic delivers a copy to every subscriber. The script on the right, infra slash ten dash fan out dot s h, creates the topic order dash events, then three queues: fulfilment, loyalty and fraud check. For each queue, a small tool sets a queue policy that lets the S N S service send to it, but only on behalf of this topic, by its A R N. Then the queue subscribes to the topic, with raw message delivery, so the queue receives the message itself rather than wrapped in S N S's envelope. The fraud check subscription also gets a filter policy, from infra slash S N S: only messages whose total attribute is five hundred or more. In the terminal, against the emulator, two orders are published, each with its total as a number attribute: o five oh one at twenty nine pounds, and o five oh five at six hundred and forty. Each publish returns a message id. Then tools slash drain dot p y reads every queue. Fulfilment has both orders. Loyalty has both. Fraud check has only o five oh five, because the filter dropped the small order for that subscription alone. The table at the bottom is that result. The publisher never needed to know that loyalty or fraud check exist: adding a fourth consumer is a new subscription, with no change to the order code. And because each consumer has its own queue, a slow fraud check never holds up fulfilment, and each one can fail and retry on its own. Next, a different way to route the same kind of message: by what happened, on an event bus.

A topic sends everything to every subscriber, trimmed by filters on attributes. An EventBridge bus works the other way round: producers put events on the bus describing what happened, and rules choose which events go where, by matching any field in the event. The script on the right, infra slash ten dash events dot s h, creates a custom bus named shop. A small function, rule, creates a queue, puts a rule on the bus with the event pattern from infra slash events, allows that rule, by its A R N, to send to the queue, and makes the queue the rule's target. Two rules are made. U K dash V A T matches events from shop dot orders, of type order placed, whose detail has country G B, and sends them to a queue named V A T ledger. Refunds matches every order refunded event and sends it to a refunds queue. In the terminal, listing the bus's rules shows both. Put events sends three sample events from a file, and the failed entry count is zero. Then draining the queues shows that V A T ledger received only o five oh one, the order placed in Great Britain, and refunds received only o four eight eight. The order placed in France, o five oh six, matched neither rule, so it went nowhere, which is correct: the bus delivers what the rules ask for, and nothing else. The table at the bottom is that matching, event by event. The list compares the two. A topic gives every subscriber each message, and filters trim it. A bus routes by what happened, from any field of the event, from many producers. On both, the publisher never lists who is listening. EventBridge also has a schema registry, which can record the shape of each event type so consumers can rely on it; the shop's events are simple enough to describe in the patterns. Next, an order that takes several steps, and what to do when one of them fails.

Placing an order really takes several steps: reserve the stock, charge the payment, ship the order. If the charge fails after the stock was reserved, the stock must be released again. Writing that in one function means writing its retries and its undo by hand. Step Functions keeps that state outside the code, in a state machine. The editor shows workflows slash place order dot A S L dot j s o n, written in the Amazon States Language. Reserve stock is a task that invokes the reserve stock function, then moves to charge payment. Charge payment invokes its function, with two rules. Retry, on line fifteen: if the error is a payment timeout, try again after two seconds, at most twice, doubling the wait each time. Catch, on line seventeen: any other error, or a timeout that outlasts its retries, is recorded in the state, and the workflow moves to release stock. The table on the right lists all five states: after charge payment comes ship order, the end; after release stock comes order failed, a fail state. In the terminal, infra slash ten dash workflow dot s h creates the state machine in the emulator, with the role order workflow, and its A R N is returned. The emulator cannot run Lambda tasks, so tools slash run workflow dot p y walks the same definition with stand in results for each task, and says so. O five oh one goes reserve, charge, ship, succeeded. O five oh seven is reserved; the charge times out, and is retried in two seconds; times out again, and is retried in four; then the card is declined, which is not a retryable error, so it is caught at six seconds, the stock is released, and the workflow ends as failed. Nothing is left reserved for an order that was never paid. The list sums it up: retry what may succeed next time, catch what will not, undo what was already done, and keep each step a small function. Next, making each of those steps safe to run twice.

A standard queue delivers every message at least once, which means sometimes twice; a retried request can arrive twice; a workflow step can be re run. So every consumer must be idempotent: running it twice has the same effect as running it once. The editor shows workers slash ship once dot p y, against the emulator. The ship function, on line sixteen, first claims a key in a Dynamo D B table named idempotency: ship hash o five oh one, put only on condition that it does not already exist. If the key is already there, line twenty returns already shipped, and the side effect, shipping, never runs a second time. Line twenty five delivers o five oh one twice, and the terminal shows shipped, then already shipped, skipped. The second half deals with a message that can never succeed: o nine nine nine, an order with an address the courier rejects. The fulfilment queue gets a redrive policy: after three receives, move the message to a dead letter queue, fulfilment dash D L Q. The worker fails three times, and on the fourth attempt the queue is empty, because the message has moved; reading the dead letter queue finds o nine nine nine. Without it, the poison message would be retried forever, at a cost, hiding real work. The last line shows retry waits with exponential backoff and full jitter: each wait is a random time up to a limit that doubles, so a thousand clients that failed together do not all retry at the same instant. The table on the right says who handles which failure. A duplicate delivery: the key, skipped. A message that never works: the D L Q after three receives, and once the cause is fixed, the messages can be redriven back and replayed. One bad message in a batch of ten: the worker reports only that one as failed, so the other nine are not repeated. A busy service: back off, with jitter. And the list: claim a key before the side effect, and treat the dead letter queue as a to do list. Next, choosing between all of these.

The map now shows the whole checkout: the order A P I, place order, the workflow, the queue, the topic and the event bus. The table at the top follows one order through it, end to end. Post slash orders is checked by A P I Gateway, and the shopper waits for that. Taking the stock and recording the order happen in place order, a Lambda function, and the shopper waits about a hundred and twenty milliseconds more. Everything after that happens without the shopper waiting. Reserve, charge and ship are a Step Functions workflow. Telling fulfilment, loyalty and fraud check is an S N S topic with three queues. The V A T ledger and refunds are EventBridge rules. And shipping it exactly once is S Q S with an idempotency key. The middle table is the choice in general. When the caller needs the answer now, use a synchronous A P I. When one consumer has work that can wait, use a queue. When several fixed consumers each need a copy, use a topic. When many producers' events must be routed by what happened, use a bus. And when the work has several steps, with retries and undo, use a workflow. These combine: in the shop, a topic feeds queues, and a workflow calls functions. The list at the bottom is what asynchronous costs, because it is not free. The shopper now sees placed, not shipped, and the page must say so honestly. Every consumer must be safe to run twice. And a failure no longer shows up as an error page in front of someone; it shows up later, in a dead letter queue, or a failed workflow, where only monitoring will notice it. That is Course twelve's job. The checkout is now decoupled: a slow courier, a fraud check or a busy loyalty service no longer slows the shopper down, and none of them can lose an order. Next, in Course eleven, the orders become data: a lake, a catalog and the questions the business asks of its sales.

The shop's managers now want to ask questions about the business: sales by day, by country, by product, over months. The orders database can answer those questions, so why not ask it? The table at the bottom is why: the database and the lake do two different jobs. The orders database holds what is true now; a lake holds everything that happened. A typical database question is order five oh one's lines; a typical lake question is sales by day and country. The database reads a few rows by key; the lake reads millions of rows but only a few columns. The database takes thousands of writes a minute; the lake is appended to in batches. And if the database is slow, checkout suffers; if the lake is slow, a report is late. The list on the right gives the reasons not to report from the orders database. A month long scan competes with checkout for the same C P U and connections. The database keeps only current state, so an order updated three times shows up once, with its last values. Its history grows forever, while its transactional tables should stay lean. And a read replica only solves the first problem, not the other two. So the shop builds a second path, shown across the top, and each step is a section of this course. The data leaves the orders database, by export or by change data capture, in section two. It lands in an S three lake as Parquet files, one folder per day, in section three. The Glue catalog records what the files mean and who may read which columns, in section four. And Athena answers S Q L over the lake, paying by the bytes it scans, in section five. Section six adds a different kind of data, a stream of clicks, and section seven asks when a warehouse or a cluster is worth it. Next, getting the data out, and proving that nothing was lost or counted twice.

There are three common ways to get data out of the orders database, listed on the right. A nightly export, for example an R D S snapshot exported to S three as Parquet, fits when a day late is fine. Change data capture, with D M S from Course nine, copies every change within minutes. And a file transfer service fits when partners send files. The shop uses change data capture, which writes one file of change records per day. The terminal shows the files for the twelfth and thirteenth of October: one J S O N record per line, each with its log sequence number, an operation, insert or update, the order, the time it was committed, and the total. The editor shows analytics slash reconcile dot p y, plain Python on local files. The naive approach, on line ten, reads the twelfth's file and sums every record: five records, nine hundred and sixty one pounds fifty. But the source database says the twelfth's orders total seven hundred and fifty six fifty. The list on the right is what a day's file is not. O five oh two appears twice with the same log position: a record replayed after a retry. O five oh three appears twice too: an insert at three hundred and forty, then an update to three hundred and fifty two fifty. And o five oh four was placed at two minutes to midnight, but its record arrived at four minutes past, so it is in the thirteenth's file. The reconciled approach, from line seventeen, reads every file, keeps each order's last change by log position, and on line twenty one puts each order on the day it was committed, not the day it arrived. That gives four orders summing to seven hundred and fifty six fifty, which matches the source exactly. Line twenty three is the habit to keep: every load is checked against a total from the source, and a mismatch stops the pipeline before a wrong number reaches a report. Next, how the history is laid out in the lake.

How files are laid out in S three decides how much every query has to read. The editor shows analytics slash layout dot p y, which writes real Parquet files on this machine, not in A W S. Parquet stores data by column, compressed, so a query that needs two columns reads two columns. History dot p y generates the shop's September: two thousand orders a day, sixty thousand rows. Then the same month is written three ways. Line thirteen writes it as one file. Lines fourteen and fifteen write it partitioned by day, in the Hive style: one folder per day, named d t equals the date, which is what Athena and Glue understand. And lines eighteen and nineteen write one day again as two hundred tiny files of ten rows each, the way a stream of small uploads would. In the terminal, the script reports sixty thousand rows over thirty days, and then what a query for one day, the twelfth of September, has to open. With one file for the month, it opens all five hundred and forty six kibibytes. Partitioned by day, it opens one folder: twenty seven kibibytes, twenty times less. As two hundred tiny files, the same day costs four hundred and thirty three kibibytes, because every Parquet file carries its own header, footer and schema, and on S three every file is also a separate request. Listing the lake shows the folders, d t equals the first, second and third of September, and inside the twelfth's folder, a single part file. The table on the right repeats the three numbers. The list gives the rules. Use Parquet, so only the columns used are read. Partition by what queries filter on, here the day. Prefer fewer, larger files, so a job compacts the small ones daily. And do not over partition: a folder per customer would be millions of tiny folders. Next, describing these files in a catalog, and deciding who may read them.

Files in S three are only bytes until something records what they mean. The Glue Data Catalog does that, and Lake Formation decides who may read what. The editor shows infra slash eleven dash catalog dot s h, run against the emulator. It creates a database, shop underscore lake, then the table order underscore history from a J S O N definition in infra slash glue: where the files are in the lake bucket, that they are Parquet, the columns and their types, and the partition key, d t. The loop registers three partitions, the eleventh to the thirteenth of September; a crawler or partition projection could find them instead. Then, from line fifteen, a Lake Formation grant: the role Analyst may select from the table, every column except customer. In the terminal, listing the partitions returns the three days. Then analytics slash add column dot p y makes a schema change, adding a column named channel. The catalog keeps both versions: version one with six columns, ending in country, and version two with seven, ending in channel. Listing Lake Formation's permissions shows the grant: the Analyst role, select, on the table with columns, excluding customer. The table on the right is what the catalog promises: where the files are, in its location; how to read them, in its Parquet serde; which columns, versioned; which days exist, as partitions; and who sees what, through Lake Formation. The list is about the schema change. It created version two of the table. Old files have no channel column, so queries see it as null for those days, which is safe. Renaming or retyping a column is not safe, because old files still carry the old name and readers break. And the Analyst never sees which customer placed an order. The emulator stores the grant but does not enforce it on queries; that is Lake Formation's documented behaviour. Next, asking the lake a question with Athena.

Athena runs S Q L directly over files in S three, using the catalog to find them, and charges for the data it scans: five dollars per terabyte in most Regions, with at least ten megabytes counted per query. The editor shows s q l slash daily sales dot s q l: for each day from the eleventh to the thirteenth of September, the number of orders and the total sales, filtered on line four by the partition column, d t. Because the filter is on the partition column, only three folders are read. The emulator can accept an Athena query but cannot run one, so the terminal runs the same S Q L file with DuckDB over the same local Parquet, and that is labelled as DuckDB, not Athena. Each day has two thousand orders: sales of one hundred and twenty four thousand three hundred and twenty five, one hundred and thirty thousand three hundred and ninety three, and one hundred and nineteen thousand and one fifty. Then the scan cost of each layout. Partitioned by day, the three days scan eighty one kibibytes; the flat file for the month scans five hundred and forty six. At this size, both are billed as the ten megabyte minimum, so the difference costs nothing. At a thousand times the data, the partitioned query would cost about four hundredths of a cent and the flat one about a quarter of a cent: six times more, on every query, every day, for every dashboard. Finally, the same S Q L file is submitted to Athena in the emulator, with the database shop underscore lake and a results location in the lake bucket, and a query execution id comes back. The table on the right sums up paying by the byte. The list is the practice: results here come from DuckDB locally; Athena was submitted to the emulator. Always filter on the partition column, and select the columns you need, never star, because Parquet then reads only those. Next, data that does not arrive in daily files at all: a stream of clicks.

Shoppers' clicks arrive continuously, thousands a second at the evening peak, and the shop wants them within seconds, not in tomorrow's file. That is a stream, and on A W S the service for it is Kinesis Data Streams, not to be confused with Data Firehose, which only delivers to a destination. In the terminal, against the emulator, infra slash eleven dash stream dot s h creates shop dash clickstream in provisioned mode with two shards, and the summary reads back two open shards and twenty four hours of retention. Then four clicks are put, with the shopper's session as the partition key: s seventeen, s twenty two, s seventeen again, and s forty one. Kinesis hashes the partition key to choose a shard, so both of s seventeen's clicks land on shard one, and within a shard, order is kept: one session's clicks are read in the order they happened. The table on the right summarises a shard. Each takes up to a thousand records a second in. Order holds within a shard. The same key always lands on the same shard. And records are kept for twenty four hours by default, and up to a year. The editor shows analytics slash consumer lag dot p y, a model, not A W S. From six to eight in the evening, eighteen hundred clicks a second arrive, and the consumer reads sixteen hundred, oldest first. Every minute, the backlog grows. The terminal prints, every half hour, the backlog and the iterator age, which is how long ago the record being read was written: four minutes at six thirty, ten at seven thirty, fourteen at eight. After eight, arrivals fall to six hundred a second, and the consumer catches up at eight twenty four. The list is what to do with that. Alarm on iterator age. If lag ever exceeds the retention period, records expire unread, which is data lost. The fixes are more shards, and more consumers. Next, when the lake needs a warehouse or a cluster behind it.

Athena is not the only engine that can read the lake. The row at the top compares three. Athena runs S Q L on S three with nothing to start or stop: it charges per terabyte scanned, a query takes seconds to minutes, and it is what the shop uses today for daily sales. Redshift is a data warehouse. It has its own fast managed storage and can also read S three, it is built for many dashboards querying all day long, and it comes provisioned, or serverless. E M R runs clusters for Spark, Hive, Presto and other frameworks, on E C two, on E K S, or serverless: it is for large transformations written as code, not for dashboards. The table at the bottom is the choice. A few queries a day over data in S three: Athena. Hundreds of dashboard queries an hour: Redshift, because a warehouse keeps data ready and is cheaper than scanning per query when queries never stop. Transforming terabytes in code: E M R with Spark. And a lakehouse platform with notebooks and scheduled jobs: Databricks on A W S, which reads the same S three. The list on the right is the caution before adding any of them. Each engine is another bill, and a provisioned one runs while idle, unless it is serverless. Each one must honour the catalog's permissions, or it becomes a way around them: an Analyst who cannot see customer in Athena should not see it in a cluster either. And Spark and Databricks each have their own course in this series, which pick up exactly where this one stops, with the same lake. That completes the shop's data: orders captured with their history, laid out by day, described in a catalog with column level permissions, queried by the byte, and clicks streamed in seconds. Next, in Course twelve, the shop is operated: what it measures, what it alarms on, who changed what, and how it recovers when something breaks.

This course is about keeping the shop running, and it starts with seeing what it is doing. The map now lights CloudWatch, and the pane on the right follows one slow evening through three kinds of signal. The numbers are the shop's worked example, not a capture. At six minutes past six, the latency metric for the order A P I changed. The median, p fifty, barely moved, from a hundred and twelve to a hundred and fourteen milliseconds. But the ninety ninth percentile, p ninety nine, jumped from a hundred and thirty two milliseconds to over a second. A metric says that something changed and when, cheaply, for the whole fleet, but not which requests or why. The order A P I's logs, in CloudWatch Logs, had lines saying the connection pool was exhausted and a request waited nine hundred milliseconds; a log says what happened to one request, but not how often, unless you count. And twenty slow traces, from X Ray or OpenTelemetry, showed where each request spent its time: ninety per cent of it waiting for a database connection. A trace explains one request, but not the fleet wide picture. The second table is how they join up. Notice: the tail moved while the median did not, which only a p ninety nine metric or an alarm on it would catch. Narrow: which requests and which minute, by finding trace ids in the slow log lines. Explain: where the time went, from the trace's segments. Confirm: how many requests and since when, with a Logs Insights query counting slow lines by minute. The list is what the evening teaches. An average hides a tail, so alarm on p ninety nine, not the mean. Put a request id in every log line and every trace, or the three signals cannot be joined. And the cause was Course nine's connection pool, again: the evening's extra servers each opened their own pool. Next, deciding how good is good enough, and when to wake someone up.

An alarm is only as good as the objective behind it. The shop's objective for checkout is that ninety nine point nine per cent of requests succeed, over any thirty days. The editor shows ops slash error budget dot p y. Lines two to four state the objective, the window, and checkout's average rate of six requests a second. Line six turns them into an error budget. In the terminal: fifteen million five hundred and fifty two thousand requests in thirty days, of which fifteen thousand five hundred and fifty two may fail. That budget is permission to fail a little, for deployments and experiments, and a measure of when to stop. The loop from line ten computes the burn rate: how many times faster than allowed the budget is being spent. At point one per cent errors the burn is one, and the budget lasts exactly the window. At two per cent, the burn is twenty, and the budget is gone in thirty six hours. At ten per cent, it is a hundred, and gone in seven point two hours. Line fifteen picks when to page a person: only for a fast burn, about fourteen times, sustained for five minutes, which at six requests a second is more than five server errors a minute. In the terminal, infra slash twelve dash alarm dot s h creates an S N S topic, ops pager, and a CloudWatch alarm named checkout five x x fast burn, on A P I Gateway's five x x error metric for the shop's A P I and stage. Reading it back gives the metric, a threshold of five, five data points to alarm, and its state, O K. The list on the right is the alarm's design. More than five a minute, in five of five minutes, so one bad minute does not page anyone. It pages ops pager, a person. A slow burn deserves a ticket for working hours, not a page at night. And missing data is treated as not breaching, so a quiet night is not an alarm. Next, the other kind of evidence: who did what, through the A P I.

CloudWatch answers how the shop is behaving. CloudTrail answers a different question: who called which A P I, when, and from where. Every action in A W S is an A P I call, as Course two showed, so CloudTrail is the record of every change. In the terminal, infra slash twelve dash trail dot s h creates a trail named shop trail, for every Region, delivering to an S three bucket, and starts it logging. Its event selectors add data events, the object level reads and writes, but only for the reports bucket, because data events cost extra and most buckets do not need them. Reading back shows the trail is logging, and that the selector covers the reports bucket. Without a trail, the console's event history still keeps ninety days of management events; with one, they are kept in S three for as long as the shop chooses. The editor shows ops slash who changed dot p y. Given a file of CloudTrail records and a resource name, it keeps the writes, records whose read only flag is false, that mention the resource, oldest first, and prints who, as what role, from which address. The records file is an example in CloudTrail's documented format, not a captured log, and the frame says so. Running it on the twelfth of October's records finds one write to the reports bucket: put bucket policy, at eighteen twelve and forty four seconds, by sam, through the Shop Operator permission set, from two oh three dot oh dot one one three dot twenty four. One other record is a read, which it skips. The table on the right says which evidence answers which question. Is checkout slow? CloudWatch metrics. What did the app log? CloudWatch Logs. Who changed a policy? CloudTrail. Who read a report? CloudTrail data events, only because they were selected. The list sums up: ninety days of history with no trail, years with one, data events only where selected, and the record here is an example. Next, operating the servers without logging in to them.

The shop's servers still need patching, and someone occasionally needs a shell on one. The old way is S S H keys and a bastion host; the A W S way is Systems Manager, and nobody holds a key. The script on the right, infra slash twelve dash ops dot s h, does two things against the emulator. First it creates a patch baseline named order A P I linux, for Amazon Linux twenty twenty three, which approves security patches seven days after release, and registers it for the patch group order A P I, the tag the app servers carry. Patch Manager then installs approved patches in a maintenance window, server by server. Second, it starts an A W S Config recorder and adds a Config rule, s three no public read, from a J S O N file. It uses the A W S managed rule that checks every bucket for public read access. In the terminal, reading back finds the baseline for Amazon Linux twenty twenty three, and the Config rule, active. The emulator stores both, but it cannot read the patch group back or evaluate compliance, so what happens next comes from the documentation. The table at the bottom is operating a fleet without logging in to it. How do I get a shell on app two? Session Manager: through the agent and the instance role, with no S S H port open and every session logged. Are the servers patched? Patch Manager, with this baseline and the order A P I patch group. What is installed where? Systems Manager Inventory. Is any bucket public? The Config rule, which records each bucket as compliant or not, and can trigger a fix. Notice that this is Course four's lesson applied to operations: people get access through roles, temporarily, and every action is recorded, rather than through long lived keys copied onto laptops. Next, the keys that protect the shop's data, and a rotation that broke a connection.

Course eight encrypted the reports bucket with a K M S key; this section looks at that key's policy, and at what rotation does to a running app. The editor shows policies slash reports key dot j s o n. A key policy is the main control on a K M S key: without it, not even the account can use the key. The first statement lets the production account administer the key, which delegates the decision to I A M policies in that account. The second lets the Auditor role in the audit account decrypt, but only through S three in E U west two, by the condition on K M S via service: the Auditor can read reports, but cannot decrypt anything directly. In the terminal, infra slash twelve dash keys dot s h creates the key with that policy, the alias shop reports, and turns on automatic yearly rotation. Then application encryption. A short text is encrypted with the key and an encryption context, report equals daily: extra data that is not secret, but must match exactly to decrypt. Decrypting with the same context returns the text. Decrypting with report equals monthly fails, invalid ciphertext, which stops a blob being reused in the wrong place. Then ops slash rotation dot p y, against the emulator's Secrets Manager and a stand in database. At nine o'clock the app reads the password once and connects. At nine thirty, rotation writes a new password and the database changes too. The app's next connection uses its cached copy and fails. On that failure it re reads the secret and, at nine thirty one, connects. The table on the right is the key in four lines. The list is the lesson: a cached password stops working at rotation, so re read the secret on an authentication failure, or rotate between two database users alternately, so the old password stays valid until every server has moved on. The database here is a stand in. Next, the layers between the internet and an order, and which of them only detect.

The map now lights W A F at the edge. The first table is every layer between the internet and an order, and the column that matters is the last: prevents or detects. Network floods are absorbed by Shield Standard, which protects every A W S account automatically; Shield Advanced adds response support and cost protection for a fee. Bad H T T P requests are blocked by a W A F web A C L. Who may reach what is decided by security groups, from Course five. Who may call what is decided by I A M and service control policies, from Course four. Those four prevent. The last two detect. GuardDuty reads CloudTrail, V P C flow logs and D N S logs, and reports credentials used in odd ways or instances talking to known bad addresses. Security Hub gathers findings from GuardDuty and other services into one place, and checks the accounts against security standards. The second table is the web A C L the shop puts on its load balancer, named shop dash web. The A W S managed common rule set blocks well known exploit patterns. A rate based rule blocks any single address sending more than a thousand requests in five minutes, so one address cannot flood checkout. Anything else is allowed. The list is the reason detection matters. Every preventing layer can be misconfigured or bypassed, and when prevention fails, it fails quietly: a wrong security group just lets traffic in. A detector is only useful if its finding reaches a person, so GuardDuty's findings are routed to the same ops pager as the checkout alarm. And in the next section, it is GuardDuty that notices the order A P I's credentials being used from somewhere they should never be. Next, that incident, minute by minute.

At eighteen nineteen on the twelfth of October, GuardDuty reports that the order A P I role's temporary credentials are being used from one nine eight dot five one dot one hundred dot sixty six, an address that is not the shop's. The table on the right is the incident's timeline. At eighteen twenty one, sam takes the lead and alex keeps notes: one person decides, one person writes. The terminal starts with the runbook, runbooks slash leaked keys dot m d, which the shop wrote before it needed it, and which names its owner: the on call operator. Its five steps are detect, lead, contain, preserve and eradicate. Containing comes before explaining. Temporary credentials cannot be revoked one by one, but they can all be made useless. The editor shows policies slash revoke sessions dot j s o n: a single deny statement, for every action on every resource, on condition that the session's token was issued before eighteen twenty. Attached to the role, it stops every session issued before then, including the stolen one, while servers that assume the role afresh get new sessions and keep working. This is what the I A M console's revoke active sessions button does. In the terminal, at eighteen twenty four, the policy is put on the order A P I role, and listing the role's inline policies shows it in place. The emulator stores it, but does not evaluate the condition, so that behaviour comes from the I A M documentation. At eighteen thirty, evidence is preserved: CloudTrail logs copied and the affected disks snapshotted, before anything is cleaned up. And at nineteen ten, the cause is found and fixed, and anything the credentials could reach is rotated. The list sums it up. Stolen sessions stop, new ones work. The calls came from one nine eight dot five one dot one hundred dot sixty six, not from the shop. And the runbook named an owner, so nobody had to ask who was in charge. Next, backups, and proving that they restore.

The shop has backups; the question this section asks is whether they restore, and how long it takes. The table on the right is the backup plan, shop daily. Every night at two A M U T C, A W S Backup copies the shop's databases and volumes into the vault shop prod vault, and keeps them thirty five days. Each backup is also copied to a vault named shop isolated, in the audit account and in E U west one, and kept ninety days, so a mistake or an attacker in the production account cannot delete every copy. In the terminal, infra slash twelve dash backup dot s h creates the vault and the plan, and reading the plan back shows that copy destination. The emulator stores the plan but takes no backups. The editor shows ops slash restore drill dot p y, last month's drill, timed against the objectives it must meet: a recovery time objective of ninety minutes, and a recovery point objective of fifteen. The times are the drill's log; the script checks them. At two o'clock the drill begins, restoring the orders database to a point in time, one fifty two. At two forty one the new instance is available. At two fifty two the app has been pointed at it and the smoke tests pass. And at three oh six, the order counts match the last export, so the data, not just the server, is right. Recovery took sixty six minutes, against ninety: met. And the restore point was eight minutes before the failure, against fifteen: met. The list is the habit. An untested backup is a hope, not a backup. Time the restore and compare it with the R T O, because that is what the business was promised. Check the data, not just that the database boots. And keep a copy that production cannot delete. A W S Backup can also run restore tests on a schedule. Next, what happens when it is not a database that fails, but a whole Region.

Two numbers frame every recovery plan. The recovery point objective, R P O, is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. The recovery time objective, R T O, is how long you can afford to be down. The table at the top is A W S's four disaster recovery strategies, cheapest first, for losing a whole Region. Backup and restore keeps only backups in the second Region: recovery takes hours, and you lose everything since the last backup, but it costs only storage. Pilot light keeps the data replicated into the second Region with the servers switched off: tens of minutes to recover, seconds to minutes of data lost, for the cost of the data copies. Warm standby runs everything in the second Region, scaled down: minutes, and seconds of data, for the cost of a small second shop. And multi site active active runs both Regions taking traffic: near zero for both, for the cost of two shops, plus the hard problem of the same data being written in two places, which Course thirteen returns to. The row at the bottom is the rest of a plan. Recover in dependency order: accounts, keys and D N S first, then the network, then the orders database, then the app, then the A P I and queues, and last the lake and reports. A plan that restores the app before its database just restores errors. The shop's objectives differ by part: checkout has an R T O of ninety minutes and an R P O of fifteen, which section eight's drill met inside one Region, at sixty six and eight; reports can wait a day. So different parts can use different strategies. And failover is only half of it: failing back is a second migration, because data written in the second Region must come home, and rehearsing only the failover means neither direction is really tested. Next, the limits A W S itself puts on the shop, and how to fail gracefully against them.

Every A W S account has quotas, and every A P I has a rate limit. The table on the right separates the kinds. An adjustable quota, such as V P Cs per Region, can be raised by request, and the time to ask is weeks before the peak, not during it. A fixed limit cannot be raised, so the design has to work within it. And an A P I rate limit answers with throttling, four two nine or a throttling exception, which the caller must handle. In the terminal, Service Quotas lists the defaults; the emulator only implements the V P C ones. Most are adjustable, at five per Region, like V P Cs, internet gateways and N A T gateways per zone. Two are fixed: the characters allowed in a V P C endpoint policy, and how many hours a peering request lasts. The editor shows ops slash backoff jitter dot p y, a model. A hundred clients are throttled at the same moment, against a service that accepts two hundred calls a second. Each throttled client backs off, doubling its wait each time, line twenty one. Without jitter, line twenty two waits exactly that time, so every client that collided retries at the same instant and collides again. With full jitter, each waits a random time up to that limit. In the terminal, without jitter the hundred clients take eight hundred and sixty five seconds and two thousand five hundred and fifty calls, with up to ninety eight landing in one ten millisecond slot. With full jitter, they are all served in one point six seconds, with two hundred and ninety five calls, and at most thirteen in a slot. The A W S S D Ks already retry with backoff and jitter; the lesson is for any retry the shop writes itself. The list sums up: retries in step collide again; jitter spreads them; and failures should be tested on purpose, with A W S Fault Injection Service, before a real one does it. Watch quotas before the peak. That completes operating the shop. Next, in the final course, the shop is measured, tuned, costed and evolved.

This last course measures the shop, tunes it, costs it and decides how it should evolve, and it starts with a rule: measure before tuning. The editor shows evolve slash saturation dot p y, a simulation, not A W S, of one app server as a queue: fifteen workers, each request needing about a hundred milliseconds of work, arriving at random. Line fourteen draws the next arrival; line fifteen makes it wait for the first free worker; line sixteen draws its work time. Line twenty two works out the server's capacity: fifteen workers at a hundred milliseconds is a hundred and fifty requests a second, if it were never idle. Then the loop raises the arrival rate and records the median and the ninety ninth percentile. In the terminal, at sixty requests a second the server is forty per cent busy, the median is ninety two milliseconds and p ninety nine two hundred and fifty one. At a hundred and twenty, eighty per cent busy, almost nothing changes: ninety nine and two hundred and sixty two. At a hundred and forty, ninety three per cent busy, the median rises to a hundred and twenty eight and p ninety nine to three hundred and forty two. And at a hundred and forty seven, ninety eight per cent busy, the median doubles to two hundred and six, and p ninety nine reaches six hundred and fourteen. That bend is the knee: past it, a little more load costs a lot of latency, and the tail goes first. The table on the right says where saturation shows first: in the percentiles, while throughput simply flattens at what the server can do, and C P U sits near a hundred per cent. The list is the practice. Measure percentiles, never only the mean. Find the knee, here past ninety per cent busy. Plan capacity to run below it, which is section three. And remember this one is a simulation. Next, taking load off the servers altogether, at the edge.

The map now lights CloudFront, in front of the load balancer. A shopper in Sydney is a long way from London, and every round trip costs time. In the terminal, infra slash thirteen dash C D N dot s h creates a CloudFront distribution in the emulator, with the shop's load balancer as its origin, and returns its id and its cloudfront dot net domain name. Reading its cache settings back shows a minimum time to live of zero, a default of sixty seconds and a maximum of three hundred, and a cache key that includes the lang query string. Then evolve slash edge latency dot p y, a model with assumed round trips: two hundred and eighty milliseconds from Sydney to London, twelve to the Sydney edge location. Loading the page directly from London takes nine hundred and fifty two milliseconds, because connecting securely and asking costs three round trips. From the edge, a cache hit takes thirty eight. A miss takes four hundred and twenty eight, because the edge must ask London once, over a connection it keeps open. With ninety per cent hits, the average is seventy seven milliseconds. The table is the cache key: what makes two requests the same page. The path, slash products slash p one thousand and one, is in it, because a different product is a different page. The lang query string is in it, because the page is translated. A tracking parameter is not, because it would split the cache into thousands of copies of one page. And cookies are not, because a shopper's cart must never be cached and served to someone else. The list is about freshness. With a default of sixty seconds, a price change shows within a minute. An urgent change can be pushed out with an invalidation. And checkout and the cart are never cached at all. The emulator supports only the older forwarded values settings used here; on A W S, the same keys and times are now set in a cache policy. Next, sizing the servers that are left.

Every server hour that does no work is paid for anyway. The table on the right is one day of the shop's demand: sixty requests a second overnight, needing one large server; two hundred and forty in the day, needing two; and five hundred and sixty in the evening, needing four, at a hundred and fifty requests a second each. The editor shows evolve slash capacity plans dot p y, which prices four ways of providing that capacity, in large server hours a day; a medium server is assumed to be half a large at half the price. Line thirteen, for the fixed plan, uses the evening's peak all day. Line fourteen works out how many servers of a size each period needs. Lines fifteen and sixteen make a plan safe against losing an Availability Zone: with three zones, losing one leaves two thirds, so the plan rounds up to three servers for every two it needs. In the terminal: four large servers all day is ninety six large hours, only forty three per cent busy. Elastic with no reserve, scaling to exactly what is needed, is fifty two hours and eighty per cent busy, but it does not survive losing a zone at the peak. AZ safe with large servers, which is the Auto Scaling group from Course six, three rising to six, is ninety hours and forty six per cent busy. And AZ safe with medium servers is seventy eight hours, fifty three per cent busy, and still survives a zone. The list says why. In the fixed plan, more than half the hours are idle. The elastic plan is the busiest, but not safe. Smaller servers give finer steps, so less capacity is held in reserve: the medium plan saves twelve large hours a day without giving up zone safety. And from section one, the plan keeps every server below the knee. Next, finding out who is spending what, and catching a mistake in the bill.

A bill is only useful if each line has an owner. The shop tags every resource with env, prod or dev, and activates env as a cost allocation tag, so the billing data carries it. The editor shows evolve slash cost lines dot p y, which reads a week of cost lines from cost slash week dot c s v, an example file in the shape of a cost report. Line ten adds up the cost by env tag, calling lines with no tag untagged. In the terminal, prod spent a hundred and forty nine dollars thirty five, ninety three per cent; dev eight dollars five, five per cent; and untagged three dollars twenty two, two per cent, which nobody owns yet. Then from line seventeen, each line's daily costs are compared with that line's median day, and any day more than three times the median is flagged. One is: the N A T gateway on the ninth of October cost forty two dollars twenty, against a median of three eighty. The table on the right is the investigation: seven hundred and sixty eight extra gigabytes went through the N A T gateway that day, because a job copied files to S three through it, and the fix is an S three gateway endpoint, from Course five, which carries that traffic privately and without the per gigabyte charge. Cost Explorer and anomaly detection do this on A W S; the script shows the idea on a file. Then infra slash thirteen dash budget dot s h creates a budget, shop prod monthly: four hundred dollars a month, for env equals prod only, with an email when the forecast passes eighty per cent. Using less is usually cheaper, but sustainability is its own pillar, and each lever has a constraint it must keep. The editor shows evolve slash footprint dot p y. The script prints all three: ninety to seventy eight large hours a day, seven hundred and thirty to sixty gigabytes, and nine hundred to ninety gigabytes a month. Data kept is data stored, on disks, somewhere, forever, unless it is deleted on purpose. These are proxies here, not carbon. And Graviton uses less energy for each request. Next, writing down a decision, and the alternatives it rejected.

The shop has grown, and its next big decision is how to run the order A P I. Decisions like this are forgotten unless they are written down, so the shop keeps architecture decision records. The decision: E C S Fargate for the A P I, R D S PostgreSQL Multi A Z unchanged. The consequences record the price as well as the gain: no more operating system patching, but a higher price per v C P U hour than committed E C two, watched monthly. The table on the right is the requirement set. Two are musts, and a must rejects an option outright: PostgreSQL transactions, and the team can run it. Three are wants, weighted: no operating system patching at three times, cost at today's load at twice, and five times peak headroom at twice. In the terminal, evolve slash score options dot p y applies them: Lambda and Dynamo D B fails a must, as does E K S. Of the rest, Fargate scores twenty nine of thirty five, and E C two nineteen. The list says why this is written down: musts reject first, wants rank what is left, and the record says when to think again. Next, the three ways to run the shop, compared on one requirement set.

The map shows the finished shop, and the first table runs its order A P I three ways. On virtual machines, E C two in an Auto Scaling group, the unit is a server; the shop patches the operating system; it scales in minutes; every server costs money while idle; at steady load, with a commitment, it is the cheapest; and every server keeps its own pool of database connections. In containers, E C S Fargate, the unit is a task; A W S patches the operating system; it scales in about a minute; every running task costs money while idle; it is in the middle on price; and every task keeps its own pool. On serverless, Lambda, the unit is an invocation; A W S patches everything; it scales in milliseconds; nothing costs money while idle; at steady load it is the dearest per request; and because thousands of short lived environments cannot each hold database connections, it needs R D S Proxy in front of PostgreSQL. The second table is what has to change when the shop moves. From E C two to Fargate: the code stays the same container image; the database is unchanged; deploys become task definitions; and the load balancer gets a new target group, which section ten uses. From Fargate to Lambda: the code is split into handlers; the database goes behind R D S Proxy; deploys become function versions; and A P I Gateway replaces the load balancer. The list is the shop's answer today, which is A D R seven's: E C S Fargate for the order A P I, because it is the same image with no patching. Lambda stays where it already fits, in place order and the order workflow from Course ten, where load is bursty and the work is short. And E C two is still the cheapest for steady load; it loses on patching, which is a cost too, paid in people's time. Next, whether the shop should run in more than one Region.

The shop survives losing an Availability Zone today. Surviving the loss of a whole Region is a different, and more expensive, decision. The editor shows evolve slash region failure dot p y, a model with stated assumptions: London fails at eighteen forty, a second Region holds an asynchronous copy of the data two seconds behind, the shop takes six orders a second, and Route fifty three checks health every thirty seconds. Line six works out what is lost. Replication between Regions is asynchronous, so orders committed in London in the last two seconds have not been copied: about twelve orders lost at failover. That is the R P O. Line eight works out how long until shoppers move. The health check needs three failures, ninety seconds, and then D N S answers already cached by browsers live for their sixty second time to live: a hundred and fifty seconds. In the terminal, a Route fifty three health check is created in the emulator with exactly those settings, thirty seconds and three failures. Then the last case, from line thirteen: active active, where both Regions take orders at once. Each Region's copy of p one thousand and two's stock still says one, because they have not synchronised yet, so the last unit is sold in London and in Ireland: one unit, two orders. Course nine's conditional writes only protect one copy of the data. The table on the right is how far to spread. One zone survives nothing. Three zones survive a zone, which is the shop today. Two Regions survive a Region, at the cost of a second shop, lost orders at failover and, if both write, conflicts. The list sums up: asynchronous means the lag is lost; D N S takes a hundred and fifty seconds to move people; two writers can sell one unit twice. For now the shop's answer is Multi A Z, with section eight of Course twelve's backups copied to another Region. Next, moving the order A P I to Fargate without stopping the shop.

A D R seven decided to move the order A P I from E C two to E C S Fargate. This section moves it without a big bang. The script on the right, infra slash thirteen dash cutover dot s h, finds the load balancer's H T T P S listener and the two target groups, shop app for the E C two servers and shop E C S for the Fargate tasks, and sets the listener's default action to forward to both, with the weights given. In the terminal, against the emulator, the weights move ninety to ten, then fifty to fifty, then zero to a hundred: all checkout traffic on Fargate. Each step has a gate. Evolve slash cutover gates dot p y checks that every order the new path acknowledged is actually stored in the orders database; the counts are the cutover's log, an example. At ninety ten, a hundred and twenty one acknowledged and a hundred and twenty one stored: pass. At fifty fifty, six hundred and four of six hundred and four: pass. At a hundred per cent, one thousand two hundred and ten acknowledged but only one thousand two hundred and seven stored: three missing. So the gate rolls back: the last command moves the weights back to fifty fifty, in seconds, while the three orders are replayed from the queue and the cause is found. The table is the rollback boundaries, which decide how cheap a rollback is. While both paths still run, rolling back is moving a weight, seconds. Once the E C two servers are terminated, it is a redeploy, about an hour. And once the new path writes a new database schema, it is a data migration, days. So the old path is kept running, and the schema left alone, until the new path has passed its gates for long enough. Moving the weight is easy; the gates are what make it safe.
